#110541. The White House confirmed a raft of new tariffs on the same day inflation data came back at nearly twice the Fed’s target

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (652 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

The White House confirmed a raft of new tariffs on the same day inflation data came back at nearly twice the Fed’s target

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The White House has unveiled a litany of new tariffs targeting imports from 14 economies, including key trading partners such as China and the EU.
  • According to recent reports, the announcement has two key implications.
  • Recent findings suggest that and second, it complicates the Federal Reserve’s next move.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The White House has unveiled a litany of new tariffs targeting imports from 14 economies, including key trading partners such as China and the EU. With consumers already stretched by an affordability crisis, the new duties come on the same day that the Bureau of Economic Analysis confirmed inflation hit 3.8%, according to the annual rate of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, and nearly double the Federal Open Market Committee’s 2% goal.

According to recent reports, the announcement has two key implications. First, though the latest duties would be imposed on foreign economies, previous tariff studies indicate that 90% of the increased prices are ultimately borne by U.S. businesses and, more often than not, their consumers.

Recent findings suggest that and second, it complicates the Federal Reserve’s next move. The Fed, now led by Kevin Warsh, raised rates in September for the first time since July 2023, to a range of 3.75% to 4%, and meets again Dec. 9–10.

Recent findings suggest that former Fed chairman Jerome Powell remarked that while tariffs represented a one-off price increase rather than broader inflationary factors, they nonetheless increased near-term inflation expectations. As UBS chief economist Paul Donovan told clients today: “The concern is the impact on U.S. inflation, and thus U.S. interest rates.”.

And the Fed already has a data headache on its hands: The PCE increase to 3.8% compared with a year ago is nearly double the FOMC’s 2% target.

Industry observers note that china faces a new 20% duty, and Vietnam, up to 35%, or 20% if it reaches a trade deal, according to Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, citing Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. Section 301 allows the U.S. to investigate foreign practices deemed unreasonable or discriminatory, or that burden or restrict U.S. commerce. Both nations are among the top 10 importers to the U.S., accounting for 7.8% and 7.4% of imports, respectively, per Census Bureau data.

Industry observers note that through September, the U.S. imported $215 billion in Chinese goods and $204.8 billion from Vietnam, which accounts for the largest U.S. trade deficit with any country, at $190.9 billion.

The European Union is also facing tariffs of 15%, while India is facing rates of up to 25%, or 17% in the event of a trade deal.

The latest revenue-generating tariff action comes after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s sweeping emergency tariffs in February, forcing the administration to refund roughly $100 billion of the $166 billion it had collected.

According to recent reports, for most of the 14 economies, existing Section 301 duties count toward the new rate rather than being added on top. (China is the exception: Its 20% stacks on existing levies.) “In effect, it’ll look more like a top-up,” Greer told CNBC’s Squawk Box. “When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points.”.

That will do little to calm the nerves of consumers who have been battling above-target inflation for more than five years. The New York Fed’s October survey of consumer expectations revealed that households expect inflation to be at 3.9% this time next year, and at 3.3% in three years’ time.

For the Fed, these heightened expectations can be a problem. Consumers may adjust their spending and saving, and make wage demands in response to their inflation expectations. That can create a self-reinforcing cycle, making inflation harder to bring down.

“The tariffs replace the previously revealed Section 301 tariffs with a marginal incremental impact higher on goods prices but, moreover, set the table for further increases if negotiations break down,” Bradford Smith, portfolio manager at Janus Henderson Investors, told Fortune in a note.

“The announcement serves as a reminder that the Fed’s inflation fight is exacerbated by tariffs. With inflation already an concern and the Fed awaiting the lapping of previous tariff implementations, additional tariffs will make the Fed’s job more difficult.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Sources indicate that one rather unusual metric on XRP Ledger has seen more than a 3,062% increase in usage which raises a lot of questions. This is one of the largest spikes throughout the year in a function usage that mostly stays low.

The function allows users to manage their secondary keys for signing transactions on their wallets and/or accounts. Their main private keys stay offline, while a certain key issued by them is used in daily transactions.

It allows safer work and utilization of their wallets without potentially exposing their private keys. So even if someone grabs hold of your signing credentials, you'll be able to protect your funds by nullifying the issued keys, provided you still retain authorized access.

Sources indicate that one way or another, the surge is bizarre. Most likely "legit" scenarios are: automated key rotations among large custodians like exchanges. Some security warnings that triggered massive migration and then, the illicit one: generation of function calls from bots or automated scripts.

Recent findings suggest that the flatlined chart actually represents tens or hundreds of calls daily, but a surge to nearly 4,000 is certainly out of the blue. Unfortunately, we were unable to identify the source of those transactions.

Recent findings suggest that the feature itself is legitimate, so the spike alone does not indicate that users' funds or wallets are at risk. However, an undisclosed exploit or security problem cannot be ruled out without further investigation.

One concerning scenario would involve malicious actors gaining access to wallets and assigning latest regular keys to maintain control over them. This would not necessarily mean that the XRP Ledger itself has been compromised, but rather that individual accounts may have been targeted.

For now, there is no evidence pointing toward such an attack, and the activity could just as easily be attributed to routine security operations.

Still, XRP holders should keep an eye on any unexpected changes to their account settings, especially regular keys they did not authorize.

Whether this was a coordinated security upgrade, automated activity, or something more concerning remains unclear. What is certain is that such an unusual spike deserves closer attention, particularly if similar activity continues over the coming days.

Microsoft’s Brad Smith on Trump’s data center tax threat: ‘You can’t support Helsinki from Upcoming Jersey’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am.
  • Recent findings suggest that microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S.
  • Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith mentioned the president is “making an vital point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith mentioned the president is “making an vital point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he mentioned most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from Fresh Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he noted.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which indicates it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

In a recent development, his reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”.

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu.

Sources indicate that he gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he mentioned. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”.

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

It has been revealed that his one example was an unnamed company that wants to build in Finland. Google confirmed a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, stated he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, remarked he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a substantial technology transfer offshore.”.

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, noted Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the firm for a briefing.

Smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate organization, and mentioned Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

White House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

It has been revealed that smith remarked Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that he put the ballroom donation in the first category, and said the company “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for issues it considered crucial.

In a recent development, outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He said the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he mentioned much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.).

According to recent reports, smith said the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the tech giant remarked.
  • Sources indicate that the startup came out of stealth in August.
  • Corma isn’t the only firm using AI to play defense.

Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the tech giant remarked. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.

Sources indicate that the startup came out of stealth in August. Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP, a popular web programming language. Another flaw was found in Node.js, the open source JavaScript runtime environment. Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident. Other incidents were disclosed that day, too. The day showcased the kind of onslaught on security that AI has enabled.

Corma isn’t the only firm using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s newly introduced startup Armadin, as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection.

It has been revealed that the story is a bit nuts. Earl started out as a real squirrel that Universal Orlando employees found nesting in a Christmas tree in 2008, where he was hoarding the blue bulbs. Staffers made him an inside joke and hid a plush squirrel in the tree every year after that.

Then a holiday store display had an empty section. Designers turned it into a Christmas tree farm owned by the squirrel and drew a cartoon version of Earl. Fans loved it, and Universal rushed out Earl merchandise that sold out fast.

Because Earl didn’t come from a film or a licensing deal, Universal owns him outright. It’s now investing in more original characters like the zombie teddy bear HamiKuma.

Sources indicate that universal pitched the balloon to Macy’s, its partner on an in-park holiday parade. “Earl, at first glance, you can’t help but to laugh,” parade executive producer Will Coss tells the Journal. Universal has even considered making movies and TV highlights starring its homegrown characters.

#110535. How Qualcomm’s CMO is reshaping his team for its post-Apple era

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1124 w)

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

How Qualcomm’s CMO is reshaping his team for its post-Apple era

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The iPhone 18, released in September, was the first of Apple’s flagship models to use its in-house C2 cellular modem.
  • “You take us out, and your iPhone becomes an iPod, basically,” Don McGuire, Qualcomm’s chief marketing officer, says, explaining how its chips work.
  • While he adds that the company knew that the end of Apple’s reliance on Qualcomm’s chips was coming, chief executive Cristiano Amon reported that revenue from Apple products would decline faster than expected, because of supply constraints.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iPhone 18, released in September, was the first of Apple’s flagship models to use its in-house C2 cellular modem. It marked the end of a 15-year arrangement with U.S. chipmaker Qualcomm, whose chips had been used in every iPhone since the iPhone 4, excluding some of Apple’s budget “e” series, to connect the devices to a mobile network.

“You take us out, and your iPhone becomes an iPod, basically,” Don McGuire, Qualcomm’s chief marketing officer, says, explaining how its chips work.

While he adds that the company knew that the end of Apple’s reliance on Qualcomm’s chips was coming, chief executive Cristiano Amon reported that revenue from Apple products would decline faster than expected, because of supply constraints.

In the year to September, Qualcomm’s total revenue fell 3% to $43.1 billion. Chip sales were down 26%, in the final three months to September.

McGuire argues the loss of Apple leaves Qualcomm less exposed to a single customer. “It’s actually very freeing when you can rebalance your customer ecosystem,” he states. In his view, Qualcomm’s success does not hinge on whether its chips end up in one phone maker’s handsets. “Are we in the iPhone? Are we not in the iPhone? I don’t care.”.

Industry observers note that the company has meanwhile sought expansion beyond the smartphone category into the laptop, car, smart-home device, wearables, and data center markets. Revenue outside of Qualcomm’s mobile chip business is anticipated to grow by more than 60% in 2027.

Data centers remain a lucrative market for chipmakers, but it’s at the moment dominated by Nvidia, whose data center business accounted for 92% of revenues in its latest quarterly results.

In June, Qualcomm unveiled a latest line of data center chips, and it is targeting $5 billion in data center revenue in 2027.

As CMO, McGuire has to persuade carmakers, computer manufacturers, and cloud companies to buy chips from a business best known for making phone modems. “We’ve diversified so much and expanded our portfolio of where we play in markets that historically we may not have been used to,” he claims. “It’s given us a really great opportunity, but it’s also obviously presented some challenges.”.

To manage that, he split Qualcomm into three brands, each covering a different chip depending on the buyer. Snapdragon is the firm’s consumer brand, covering the processors inside phones, laptops, and cars. Dragonwing is Qualcomm’s industrial and robotics brand, and Dragonfly, debuted in June, covers Qualcomm’s data center products, including server processors and AI chips.

Qualcomm sells to device makers, rather than consumers. However, there is still an advantage to marketing to the broader public. The more people look for a Snapdragon laptop, the more chips Dell, Samsung, and others order, McGuire explains.

“Are we in the iPhone? Are we not in the iPhone? I don’t care.”.

In a recent development, this is why the brand has focused on building partnerships with sports teams, including a sponsorship deal with Manchester United, which McGuire notes delivers exposure equal to 42 Super Bowl ads a season, and its partnership with the Mercedes Formula 1 team. McGuire says the aim is to make technology “visible and emotionally resonant.”.

This year’s holiday ad, which sees a father build a time machine using Qualcomm’s chips so his impatient son can travel forward through time to Christmas morning, takes a similar approach.

Sources indicate that “People don’t care about specs, speeds, or feeds,” McGuire says. “They care about what technology can do for them, and they care about their passions.”.

Industry observers note that data center customers are a different audience, however. The people signing off on Qualcomm’s server chips are cloud companies and finance chiefs, for whom cost matters most. Here, Qualcomm competes with Nvidia on price and power use, a growing concern as data centers’ electricity demands rise. “Nobody does performance per watt better than we do,” McGuire states. Qualcomm has already signed Meta and AWS.

Running separate brands across so many markets has also stretched McGuire’s team, which he says has not grown as fast as the tech giant’s ambitions.

Recent findings suggest that mcGuire wants his team to spend 75% of its time on planned work and 25% on what he calls “dive and catch,” meaning urgent, last-minute requests. By last year, those figures had flipped, and most of the team’s time was spent firefighting. “I knew this wasn’t going to be sustainable,” he adds.

McGuire believes AI will be crucial in enabling his small marketing team to keep pace with the growing list of demands. In January, McGuire tore up the department’s structure and rebuilt it around AI. “CMOs have a fresh role now, and that’s chief architect,” he states.

According to recent reports, “Roles we thought were going to be key three to five years ago are less important today,” McGuire adds, such as production design and copywriting, which is now handled by AI agents. Meanwhile, data, strategy, and creative direction have become more important.

According to McGuire, fewer than 5% of the marketing department was affected. Most of those people moved into fresh roles, and a smaller number whose skills no longer matched what the team needed left. He calls it “more of a redeployment.”.

McGuire claims the upcoming structure is already paying off, helping to lower the tech giant’s reliance on agencies and reduce cycle times by two-thirds.

Industry observers note that despite all the changes, McGuire expects further upheaval in the near future. “It’s probably only going to last us 24 months. Technology is changing so fast, I’m not so naive as to think we’ve got another five years,” he adds.

His previous structure, designed in 2021, was meant to last five years but only lasted three and a half years. The department has gone from a single AI writing tool to several AI systems in three years, and McGuire sees no sign of that slowing. “Every day there’s a latest tool,” he states. “Every day they’re becoming more agentic.”.

According to recent reports, mcGuire notes that he has pushed back on demands for AI-driven cost cuts. “I don’t believe we’re at a stage right now where anyone could demand a reduction in cost because of AI,” he notes. “It’s too early for that. We’re experimenting and learning.”.

Many CMOs face similar pressures. A third of marketing leaders surveyed by executive-search firm Spencer Stuart said they expected to cut headcount within two years, through AI or by eliminating redundancies.

For Qualcomm, the challenge will be whether it can make the jump from phones to data centers, and whether its marketing can keep up. “If we believe we can disrupt, if we believe we have a better solution, we’re going to take a chance,” McGuire indicates.

Recent findings suggest that weight-loss drugs are shrinking more than waistlines. According to a upcoming Revenue Management Solutions report covered by Restaurant Business, 73% of GLP-1 consumers say they’ve cut back on fast food, more than in any other restaurant category.

Sit-down spots aren’t immune. Two-thirds of users are visiting casual-dining chains less, and 60% are pulling back on fast casual and fine dining. The lone winner is salad and bowl chains, where 48% say they’re ordering more. Desserts take the hardest hit, with 78% skipping them.

Sources indicate that nine in 10 people say they eat less per sitting. Six in 10 take half or more of their meal home, and nearly a quarter order kids’ meals. Burger King president Tom Curtis notes he’s seeing “more adults eating a kids’ meal now than I’ve seen in the past” and that the chain may need smaller portions.

Recent findings suggest that mcDonald’s sees upside. Skye Anderson, president of McDonald’s USA, told investors that 84% of households with a GLP-1 user still visit the chain. “This is an opportunity,” she said. Data firm Circana finds that restaurant spending drops in the first year on the drugs, then rebounds moderately after the second.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.
  • Since Grant Canary launched his manufacturer a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.
  • The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.

Since Grant Canary launched his manufacturer a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.

The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape. It went on to purchase three companies that collect and cultivate conifer seeds and grow saplings for planting, and rebranded as Mast Reforestation.

Industry observers note that the company recently shifted again, adding a fresh line of operations: taking scorched timber and burying it in clay-lined vaults where it won’t rot and release carbon. Biomass burial clears the woody debris — the most expensive step in forest restoration post wildfire — while also generating essential revenue by selling carbon credits. Proceeds from the sales help landowners “get their forest back,” Canary mentioned, which benefits everyone.

Recent findings suggest that just as Canary has pursued unexpected paths to forest restoration, the sustainability leader also has unconventional solutions and sources of inspiration for tackling climate change. Keep reading to learn more. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.

When did you realize you had to work in sustainability?

High school. I had a really fantastic teacher my senior year, and they got me focused on my philosophical underpinnings. I’m a utilitarian — greatest good for the greatest number of people, is how I would define that — and so my worldview formed around that time. And climate change is the problem that all other problems report to.

What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

Humans aren’t great at long-term projection. We’re much more responsive to short-term, and I am concerned that by the time that it is short-term, which is now, that there is not enough political will to understand the implications of climate change and how that affects all of the concerns.

What gives you the most hope for the planet?

When I founded what would become Mast, there were not the technologies to replace the [fossil fuel] incumbents. That was 2016. The state of EVs versus internal combustion engine cars was not there yet. It’s getting there quickly. Solar was not necessarily the cheapest. Battery was still not there. Geothermal, we didn’t have that. Now we continue to have more and more of those tools to replace the incumbents. And by the way, the “incumbents” is the corporation, not the people working for those companies.

Recent findings suggest that I very much want all of the better products and technologies. Yes, they’re sustainable, but they’re also just better. I want to brain drain all of the oil and gas companies and put them to work in geothermal.

If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

In “Ready Player Two” [a sequel to “Ready Player One,” which Steven Spielberg turned into a movie], there is a technology that allows you to step into other humans’ lived experience and feel — and not just in video form, but in the smells, in the emotions, in the feelings, and basically live out other people’s lived experience.

It has been revealed that that ability to make empathy mass scale would be a massive game changer in humans having more empathy for each other and understanding the challenges and problems that others are dealing with globally. That would be the technology that would advance things significantly.

What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

My personal infrastructure. I’m lucky enough to have bought a house a few years ago and upgraded to a heat pump; Span [electrical] panels, which sets us up for vehicle-to-grid, solar, batteries, other things; an EV; and then less glamorous but equally vital: insulation, both in the siding and in the windows and blinds. I’m sort of on my journey. We already have an electric cooktop, it’s not the amazing kind, and we have gas hot water heaters, so those are next up — and solar and batteries.

Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

It has been revealed that I would change the question and say, who would I want to work for? There’s a ton to learn from someone by working for them, and I think my answer then is [Fresh York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani. Not a sustainability leader by default, but he has accomplished and built a political backing to do big things that are ambitious, and from a sustainability lens, I would want to learn from that.

In the climate space, when we got started, the problem was [a need for more sustainable] tools. It has moved down the supply chain into execution, it’s go-to-market, and that means political will.

What’s the most overhyped climate solution right now?

Sources indicate that AI. I use it. I enjoy it. I think it’s fun. But to say that it will solve the challenges of climate in the future are complete red herrings. AI is available to both sides. It is equally as effective at making gas extraction, oil extraction cheaper, faster, etc. as it is helping sustainable technologies get off the ground, and so I would say it is a neutral technology at best.

What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

Nature as infrastructure. If people can’t get themselves to the place where they value forests for their aesthetics, for the health, for the community, for all of the other things, fine. Look at it on a spreadsheet and tell me how much it’s going to cost to replace several hundred thousand acres of forest with water treatment plants, water chiller plants, water purification plants, because that’s going to be a lot of tax dollars. And if we just let it burn, if we clear-cut it all to oblivion, that means that the city of Seattle’s water supply is not going to be as cold. It’s going to require a hell of a lot more purification, and there’s not going to be as much of it.

What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

My hope is that we’ve established the funding source for reforestation with a carbon market. The carbon market is what pulls nature as infrastructure into a valued asset. It’s not an esoteric nice-to-have from a philosophical perspective, it is a valued asset that puts it into the human system of economics in a much bigger way. A carbon market is as significant an evolutionary step for humanity as the printing press, as banking, as generally accepted accounting principles.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “We’re excited … to explore innovative ways to engage fans and strengthen their connection to the game,” said Los Angeles Lakers president and chief business officer Lon Rosen.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Los Angeles Lakers have announced a tie-up with Kalshi, becoming the latest sports team to partner with a prediction market—and leaving little doubt about where the National Basketball Association has placed its chips in the ongoing debate about the role of the controversial wagering platforms in the world of pro sports. The team announced the news on Tuesday in a brief statement that hailed the partnership, but offered few details on what it will entail.

“We’re excited … to explore innovative ways to engage fans and strengthen their connection to the game,” said Los Angeles Lakers president and chief business officer Lon Rosen.

The announcement also solidified a broader alliance between the NBA and prediction markets. The league officially embraced the platforms only a month ago, when it named Kalshi and Polymarket its preferred exchanges. Kalshi has since moved quickly to turn that opening into team-level agreements, signing the Philadelphia 76ers in October before adding the Lakers this week.

The NBA’s overall positioning came as something of a surprise, given that it and the National Football League had largely held back while other major sports leagues signed agreements with prediction markets. Some of these platforms let customers as young as 18 wager on event contracts, with sports making up the bulk of trading.

Other major sports organizations have mostly taken a welcoming approach. The National Hockey League became the first major North American professional sports league to strike prediction market deals in October 2025, signing multiyear agreements with Kalshi and Polymarket that included rights to league data, branding, and broadcast advertising. That push expanded to more teams last week, when seven NHL teams announced their own marketing deals with Novig. Others, including Major League Soccer, Major League Baseball, and UFC, have also struck deals with prediction markets.

The NFL, meanwhile, has remained as the odd one out.

In early October, the league filed a 24-page brief urging the Supreme Court to back state gambling regulators, who argue that sports prediction contracts should follow the same rules as traditional sports bets. At the heart of that dispute is whether the contracts are financial products governed by federal regulators or bets subject to state gambling laws. The league also raised concerns about cheating, insider trading, consumer protection, and risks to younger consumers.

The legal fight also hangs over the Lakers’ newly introduced partnership. California allows tribal casinos and a state lottery, but it has kept traditional sports betting off the table, with a bookmaking ban dating back more than a century. The state kept that prohibition in place after the Supreme Court cleared the way for states to legalize sports betting in 2018, and voters rejected two legalization measures in 2022.

If the Supreme Court takes up the case and sides with state regulators, Kalshi could face new limits on offering sports contracts in California—complicating its push to reach fans in the Lakers’ home market.

Long-time Shiba Inu community member and SHIB developer, Mazrael, has reacted to Solana-based memecoin platform Pump.fun's recent wallet login changes, which are sparking concerns about private key security.

In a recent development, in a latest announcement, Pump.fun stated that external wallet sign-in is being retired on November 30, 2026. Starting November 30, 2026 (15:00 UTC), Pump.fun on the web will only allow users to sign in with an email account or a Google, Apple, or GitHub account instead of an external wallet such as Phantom, Solflare, or Ledger.

Industry observers note that pump.fun reassures people that nothing will happen to their funds or account, as their wallet address, positions, callouts, followers and username remain unchanged. The only change is how users sign in.

People who sign in to their accounts with Phantom or any other wallet are urged to take action before the November 30, 2026 deadline.

In a recent development, pump.fun outlined a number of steps for users on how to switch their sign-in; of particular concern is the step that asked users to enter their wallet details and paste their private key when prompted. Pump.fun noted that this step encrypts the key in the user's browser and that the key is end-to-end encrypted by its login provider, Privy, allowing users' wallets to continue working for everything else.

Mazrael reacted to the development, drawing attention to the potential security implications for consumers.

pumpfun is retiring external wallet logins on web starting Nov 30. From then on you sign in with Google, Apple, email or GitHub. To keep your existing account..... they want you to paste your private key into their Privy flow 😬 Also note their own terms says they won’t ask for private keys...

In a recent development, the standard security practice across the cryptocurrency industry is that exchanges, wallet providers and other platforms do not ask owners to disclose their private keys or recovery phrases. Such warnings are routinely issued to protect users from unauthorized access to their funds.

The Pump.fun wallet login change process appears to contradict this widely promoted security principle, Mazrael noted.

Private keys are highly sensitive credentials that give holders direct access to their cryptocurrency wallets. Whoever gets their hands on them might be able to access those wallets and move the funds. In general, it is recommended never to share private keys with individuals, support agents or third-party services.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I was recently on a podcast and the host asked me what my lowest part of my career was,” Hank Green mused on a recent episode of his own podcast, Dear Hank & John.

That’s a tough question for anyone to answer, let alone someone who has spent about two decades regularly posting videos online for an increasingly broad audience.

“Really the low — the long low — was just watching as [the internet] went from being this lovely thing that a bunch of creatives were goofing around [on] to it being freaking everything, and mattering so much, and getting taken over by all tons of terrible vibes and algorithms selecting for outrage, and it being a huge degradation to the social order,” Green said.

That’s bleak, but Green is at least trying to lead by example in showing that we don’t have to accept that the good parts of the internet are gone forever. The notoriously entrepreneurial vlogbrother has spun up a fresh tech giant with Leslie Morgan: ClockwiseTV, a curated, ad-free educational video platform for children ages 8 to 12.

According to recent reports, “[Hank] came to me last September like, ‘I have had this idea for a really long time, and it stems from the fact that my child, who’s nine, always is asking me for five more minutes on whatever device he’s on,’” Morgan, who has spent 20 years working on the business side of the creator economy, told TechCrunch. “I was like, I have that same problem… ‘How do you contain time, but also give the child agency?’”.

Clockwise’s answer to that question seems to be this: At the start of each viewing session, the parent and child decide how long they can watch, and the platform will recommend videos that will adhere to that time frame. If a kid is in the midst of a 30-minute session and has already watched two 10-minute videos, they’re not going to be suggested a 20-minute video when they only have 10 minutes left.

The startup is addressing a pretty widespread concern among parents, who are worried about more than simply negotiating with their children about how long they can use the iPad. According to a 2025 study by the Pew Research Center, about 51% of parents of children 12 or younger say their kid watches YouTube every day, among other video apps.

Sources indicate that youTube has a dedicated app for children under 13, YouTube Kids, which offers a wide range of parental controls, but the app can reportedly still serve children a wealth of low-quality AI slop. Other apps that don’t have a kids’ version can be even worse.

Clockwise indicates it is also solving that problem by hand-curating a library of educational videos from creators like Odd Animal Specimens, Draw with Jazza, and Nerdforge, as well as channels Green had a hand in creating, like Crash Course Kids and SciShow Kids.

Sources indicate that “When you go into the app, there’s a dozen choices [of videos] that you can choose from to start,” Morgan, the startup’s CEO, remarked. “There’s search functionality as well, so you can say, ‘Hey, I’m really interested in math today,’ so you can look up Stand-up Maths and look at what’s available in that time frame.”.

Some of these creators cater to people of all ages, but Clockwise says its team manually reviews each video it uploads and edits it so that it’s ready for younger eyes. The team might remove anything from embedded product placement to what Morgan calls “spectacle power tool use.”.

In a recent development, “Simone Giertz, who’s a maker creator, tends to curse a lot. But a lot of that content is great for kids,” Morgan explains. “She makes a skateboard for her three-legged dog, and if she drops an f-bomb, we’re going to cut it out so that it’s suitable for children.”.

In a recent development, clockwise pays these creators an upfront fee to use their videos, then shares 25% of revenue based on watch time. Clockwise charges parents $6.99 per month or $69.99 per year to access the platform, which it promises will remain free of ads.

“Humans are checking [the videos] four times at least before it’s ever published into our app […] That will always stay,” Morgan said. “We’re not interested in using AI to wash down our content.”.

Sources indicate that so far, a few hundred parents have tested Clockwise with their children in beta. On Tuesday, the platform is opening to the public with apps made for iOS and Android smartphones and tablets.

The platform has not taken on any outside funding, and is funded by Green himself.

Recent findings suggest that “It was really vital that he had full control,” Morgan mentioned. “He wanted to invest his own wealth into this. That was also really important because it is something he just believes in so wholeheartedly, as do I.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.
  • Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.
  • In a recent development, amazon didn’t disclose financial terms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.

Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.

In a recent development, amazon didn’t disclose financial terms. Amazon agreed to pay about $7.5 billion for the assets, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The deal is tied to performance targets over five years, Globes reported.

The deal could boost Amazon’s push to compete with Nvidia, which sells most of the chips used for training and running AI models today. Amazon makes its own AI chips, called Trainium, and has signaled plans to start selling them directly to other companies, beyond its own AWS data centers.

“We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” CEO Andy Jassy remarked on the company’s earnings call last month.

Amazon confirmed the deal the same day Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, ending a leadership shakeup at the chipmaker that put CFO Colette Kress in the interim role.

Decart’s software is designed to get more performance out of each chip, one of the main selling points Amazon needs to win those external customers. Microsoft is building its own Maia chips, mainly for its own AI services, and Google has its TPUs.

Decart’s software has also run on chips from Nvidia and Google. Amazon didn’t say whether that will continue.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” stated Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing, in the blog post announcing the acquisition.

According to recent reports, decart’s three co-founders are joining Amazon: CEO Dean Leitersdorf, his brother Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev. Amazon isn’t buying Decart’s AI models, Bloomberg reported. Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.

The deal runs through Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip unit, and Decart’s technology will be used to improve performance on Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia AI chips, according to Globes. The Israeli business publication reported that Annapurna co-founder Nafea Bshara led the negotiations for Amazon.

The founders, who own about 64% of Decart, have committed to stay at Amazon for five years and could receive about $4.8 billion collectively, Globes reported.

Amazon bought Annapurna, also founded in Israel, in 2015 for a reported $350 million. Its engineers went on to design Trainium and Amazon’s other custom chips.

According to recent reports, amazon and Decart have worked together since 2025. Decart was among the first customers on Trainium3, and Amazon said last December that Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of GPUs.

Sources indicate that the deal follows Amazon’s release last month of TorchNeuron, a tool that runs common AI code on Trainium with minimal changes. Both moves target the software advantage that has kept developers on Nvidia hardware, as GeekWire explained when the talks surfaced in October.

Decart drew interest from other substantial buyers before Amazon. Anthropic was in talks to acquire it for about $6 billion, Bloomberg reported in August, before it walked away in September. Nvidia held earlier acquisition talks, according to CTech, and invested in Decart’s $300 million funding round in May.

According to recent reports, “From day one, our mission has been to redefine the boundaries of what AI can do and to make it dramatically more efficient along the way,” Dean Leitersdorf said in Amazon’s announcement. “Joining Amazon gives our team the scale, the customers, and the infrastructure to pursue that mission faster than we could on our own.”.

The deal is subject to regulatory clearance. Amazon didn’t say what happens to Decart’s AI models or to its existing customers, such as eBay, which is also an investor in the startup.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this Side Hustle Spotlight Q&A features Lauren Mahurin, a 32-year-old entrepreneur living in Fresh York City. Mahurin is the founder of Lohso, an organic coconut-sap soy sauce alternative with 53% less sodium. Mahurin started Lohso as a side hustle in February 2026 while working full-time leading marketing and affiliate strategy at Publicis Media for some of the biggest names in retail, including Verizon, Disney and Macy’s.

According to recent reports, six months after launching the business, she turned down a promotion and quit her corporate role to go all-in. Lohso sold out of its initial inventory in 60 days, currently sees about $15,000 in revenue a month and is available in more than 50 retailers nationwide. Responses have been edited for length and clarity.

How did you validate that people would actually pay for your product before investing serious money?Years before I launched the side hustle, I lost 100 pounds and became much more intentional about what I was eating. I loved food and cooking and had absolutely no interest in eating bland chicken and steamed vegetables for the rest of my life.

In a recent development, I started noticing how certain ingredients made me feel, especially sodium. When I looked for “better for you” options, the products either didn’t deliver on taste, or they looked and felt like something you’d find in the back corner of a health food store. I didn’t want choosing better ingredients to involve a compromise.

But I didn’t want to build something just because I thought it was a good idea. I surveyed our target demographic to understand what they were buying, what they loved, what frustrated them and what they wished existed. We also conducted blind taste tests against traditional soy sauces and other coconut aminos brands to make sure we could compete on the one thing that ultimately matters: taste.

In a recent development, which two or three essential tools, apps or pieces of gear did you buy in your first week that actually made a difference?I joke that Claude was my first employee. Except it didn’t need a salary, benefits or time off.

Industry observers note that as a bootstrapped founder working a full-time corporate job, I couldn’t afford to hire an entire team. Claude became my unofficial COO, helping me build systems, analyze operational information and streamline a lot of the behind-the-scenes work that comes with running a physical product business. Of course, I still had to make the decisions and oversee the execution, but it made operating as a team of one much more manageable.

Shopify was another nonnegotiable. I wanted to own our relationship with customers from day one rather than rely entirely on retailers to sell the product. And Canva allowed me to create marketing materials and test ideas without hiring a designer every time I needed something.

It has been revealed that what were the exact first three steps you took in your first 30 days? It took about a year to go from an idea in my head to a physical product ready to sell. Which, by the way, is a humbling experience when you have absolutely no background in food manufacturing.

There are a million moving pieces when launching a CPG brand, but three things made the biggest difference for me:.

1. Build a brand people actually want to be associated with. I knew I didn’t want Lohso to look like another health food product. I wanted someone to see it on their friend’s kitchen counter and ask, “Wait, what is that?” The branding had to be as compelling as the product itself.

It has been revealed that 2. Bring people along for the ride. Long before we introduced, I started creating founder-led content documenting the process. The wins, the mistakes, the packaging decisions, the headaches of managing an international supply chain. People weren’t just following a sauce brand; they were following the story of someone trying to build something from scratch. By the time we launched, there was already an audience invested in seeing us succeed.

It has been revealed that 3. Get the product into people’s hands. I started gifting Lohso to industry vets and creators whose opinions I genuinely trusted. No contracts, no expectations, just a product I believed in. Nearly all of them ended up posting organically, and some are still talking about Lohso eight months later. That kind of genuine enthusiasm is something you can’t manufacture with an influencer budget.

How much money did you spend upfront, and what specific tools, platforms or free resources did you use to get your first paying customer?I invested approximately $80,000 of my own money into bringing Lohso to market, primarily across product development, packaging, manufacturing and marketing.

Sources indicate that our very first paying customer came through the email newsletter announcing our launch. And that first week? Sales were beyond my wildest expectations.

We had retailers interested before we even introduced, largely because I’d been building in public. That’s what’s so exciting about starting a business today. You can build an audience, create demand and get in front of buyers before you even have a finished product. By launch day, people already felt like they were part of the journey.

Nowadays, which specific tools or platforms help you bring in customers, and what is one feature inside those tools that saves you the most time?Shopify and Meta have become two of our most notable growth tools.

We released paid advertising on Meta in July 2026, and since making that investment, we’ve doubled our sales. It’s allowed us to grow beyond our initial organic audience and introduce Lohso to people who otherwise might never have discovered us.

According to recent reports, but what I love most is the customer data we get through Meta and Shopify. Understanding who’s buying Lohso, what’s motivating her first purchase and what brings her back for a second or third order. Being able to see that behavior in Shopify’s customer reports saves me from having to piece everything together manually, and it helps us make smarter decisions about where to invest.

That information shapes everything from our advertising creative to the products we’re considering launching next.

How many months did it take to reach consistent monthly revenue? What is your current monthly revenue and profit margin?We generated revenue in our very first week and sold through our initial inventory within the first 60 days. We began investing in Meta advertising in July, and since then, we’ve seen consistent month-over-month sales growth, supported by returning customers and new customers discovering Lohso online and through retail.

One of the biggest misconceptions about entrepreneurship is that revenue equals money in your pocket. Especially in CPG, growth requires capital. You’re constantly making investments today for sales you hope to generate months down the road.

We’re right now generating approximately $15,000 in monthly revenue, and our margins vary depending on our channel mix, retail launches and ongoing investments in growth.

If someone is starting from scratch today, what is the single highest-impact action they should take this weekend, and what common beginner mistake should they avoid?Go talk to 10 people who would actually be your customers — not friends and family.

Ask them what they’re buying today, what they hate about it, what they wish existed and what would actually convince them to spend money on something different. Then listen. Really listen.

A lot of first-time founders fall in love with their idea before they’ve figured out whether anyone else wants it. They spend months perfecting a logo, obsessing over packaging, building a beautiful website and convincing themselves they’re building a business.

In a recent development, and listen, I love branding. I could spend an entire weekend debating the perfect shade of brown for a bottle cap. But a beautiful brand means nothing if nobody wants what’s inside.

Sources indicate that you don’t need to quit your job, raise a $1 million or have every answer figured out to get started. You just need to find a problem worth solving, make sure other people agree and be willing to figure out the rest as you go.

ZetaChain's 55M ZETA Burn Isn't a One-Time Event: What Proposal 2 Really Does

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments.
  • Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn.
  • Sources indicate that zetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

Sources indicate that zetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

That detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no upcoming mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain claims nothing moves unless it passes.

If it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's newly introduced private AI app, ZetaLabs, releases alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a latest whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

The snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

On Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

Sources indicate that that sequence is the strongest holder protection in the strategy, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain states it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain claims the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

It has been revealed that the biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange consumers depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

According to recent reports, scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

On the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain says it will announce any change to the process in advance.

The vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

Recent findings suggest that if it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Sources indicate that taken together, this looks more like a retirement plan for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

Thinking About a Second Location? Here Are 5 Signs You’re Ready

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • It has been revealed that A thriving first business location can make opening another feel like the obvious next move.
  • I judge business success partly by whether the business is growing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

It has been revealed that A thriving first business location can make opening another feel like the obvious next move. But before you open a second, take a hard look at what makes the first one work. Can your team repeat that success while you divide your time between two businesses?

I judge business success partly by whether the business is growing. That doesn’t mean chasing every opportunity or signing a lease just because a space becomes available. Growth should be calculated, with the people, money, and commitment to support it.

Franchise owners already have a business model to follow, but they still have to build a strong operation in each market. Here are five signs I look for in deciding whether to expand, plus one that overrides them all.

In a recent development, start with an honest look at your financials. Strong sales are encouraging, but steady profitability tells you more about whether your business is ready to expand.

Sources indicate that look beyond a great month or a busy season. Your first location should generate enough to cover operating expenses, royalties, financing obligations, and a reasonable salary for you, with money left over. Review both profitability and cash flow, since they don’t always move together.

Recent findings suggest that also, consider how the business performs during slower periods. If it needs constant cash infusions to get through normal seasonal fluctuations, strengthening that operation should come first.

Next, separate the cost of opening from the cost of getting established. You’ll need money for both.

A new location may take time to attract customers and cover its expenses. Therefore, your budget should account for startup costs, ongoing operating needs, and a cushion for delays or slower sales. Build that plan around realistic assumptions about your brand and market.

According to recent reports, before adding another unit, ask yourself what happens if it takes longer than expected to gain traction. You should be able to support the launch while protecting the original business’s working capital. Otherwise, one difficult opening could put both operations under pressure.

Sources indicate that can you leave for a week without the operation falling apart? That’s a useful test because a second business will (or should) demand a great deal of your attention.

Some of our franchise owners have told me, “Man, I left for a week, and we had our best week ever.” Once you get over the discovery that you’re not irreplaceable, take that as an encouraging sign.

Sources indicate that however, you need more than one dependable person. Look for employees who can step into leadership roles, supported by clear expectations, training, and regular reporting.

Our manufacturer has a policy of promoting leaders from within. Existing team members already know your standards and your customers. They’ll still need management training, but you’re building on an established relationship. If you hire externally, give yourself enough time to bring that person into the business before opening day.

Pay attention to where your customers live and work. A steady stream from a nearby area may suggest an opportunity to serve them closer to home.

It doesn’t prove there’s no competition, though. Nor does it guarantee enough demand to support another unit. Instead, treat those customers as a starting point for research.

Study the area’s demographics, competitors, site access and territory availability with your franchisor. Then consider whether the latest business will attract additional customers or mainly shift sales away from your first location.

You want evidence that the opportunity extends beyond a handful of enthusiastic requests to open closer to someone’s neighborhood.

Financial readiness matters, but so do your expectations. You need the patience to let a latest operation establish itself.

Recent findings suggest that when I started Signarama 40 years ago, people compared it with Minuteman Press, which my dad had founded. Minuteman had been operating for 20 years. Yet people still pointed to its higher earnings as evidence that it was the better business.

That wasn’t a useful comparison. One business had a long history; the other was just getting started.

According to recent reports, similarly, when you open a second location, measure it against realistic launch milestones. Track its progress in sales, customer retention, and operating performance. Use what you learned in the original business, while recognizing that the latest team needs time to build relationships and momentum.

Finally, you have to care enough to show up and do the work.

It has been revealed that I recently spoke with a franchise owner who had opened another location in a different state. He hadn’t visited in 90 days. He stated things were going fine, but I told him he needed to be there regularly, especially during the startup period.

It has been revealed that if you want to grow, you have to go. That’s it. You don’t have a choice. You have to be there on a consistent basis. I go to Australia every year to visit with our franchisees there, and I was in India recently for grand openings of two fresh locations for one of our brands.

All the signs about financing and staffing and market penetration mean nothing if you don’t care about doing everything you can to make your latest location a success. Are you committed to the expansion?

If you’re not committed to it, fully committed to it, don’t do it.

A thriving first business location can make opening another feel like the obvious next move. But before you open a second, take a hard look at what makes the first one work. Can your team repeat that success while you divide your time between two businesses?

I judge business success partly by whether the business is growing. That doesn’t mean chasing every opportunity or signing a lease just because a space becomes available. Growth should be calculated, with the people, money, and commitment to support it.

Recent findings suggest that franchise owners already have a business model to follow, but they still have to build a strong operation in each market. Here are five signs I look for in deciding whether to expand, plus one that overrides them all.

Science Corporation, the medical technology startup founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the company noted in a blog post.

Investors in the upcoming round valued the tech giant at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.

Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage latest technologies to understand and interact with the brain.

Sources indicate that science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialed for newly introduced conditions.

Hodak announced that the device is now being trialed for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

According to recent reports, with the funding, the manufacturer aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the U.S.

Industry observers note that still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The company is right now designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.

It has been revealed that shiba Inu (SHIB) gained 5.96% over the past 24 hours and traded at $0.0000038 on Monday, according to CoinMarketCap, as talk of a December "Santa rally" returned to the crypto market. Still, SHIB is down 8.86% over the past seven days, and the token has lost 18.5% in November so far, according to CryptoRank.

Last week, SHIB dropped to $0.00000337, its lowest level since 2021.

The hopes for a Santa rally come after Goldman Sachs analysts mentioned last week that most of the December gains on the stock market usually come after Dec. 15. SHIB's own December history, however, demonstrates that the Santa rally came for the token once in five years.

It has been revealed that according to CryptoRank, SHIB lost 29.5% and 13.5% in December of 2021 and 2022, respectively. In December of 2023, the token gained 24.6%. In December of 2024 and 2025, SHIB lost 21% and 17.6%, respectively.

SHIB's median December return is -17.6%, and its average December return is -11.4%, according to CryptoRank data.

The green December of 2023 came after SHIB gained 6.04% in October and 6.62% in November of that year, according to CryptoRank. In 2026, SHIB lost 18.6% in October, and November is also in the red so far.

The Goldman note, titled "GS Flow of Funds: Chopsgiving," came from Gail Hafif, Brian Garrett and Lee Coppersmith, who looked at S&P 500 data going back to 1928. According to the note, the index usually gains 1.1% from mid-November to early December and then gives back about two-thirds of that gain by mid-December, and around 80% of the full 2.4% gain comes after Dec. 14-15.

Industry observers note that since 1990, the S&P 500 has risen after Dec. 15 in 27 of 36 years, according to Goldman.

The Goldman team called these figures a historical map. In the years when the VIX volatility index was above 18 in the middle of November, the S&P 500 gained 1.34% on average, and the index ended the year higher in 59% of cases, according to the note. According to Goldman, the VIX was above that level in mid-November of this year as well.

Goldman also noted that retail investors have been buying big tech and chip stocks. Large funds and systematic traders have been cutting their positions, according to the note.

It has been revealed that the Stock Trader's Almanac counts the last five trading days of December and the first two trading days of January as the Santa Claus rally. This season, the window will open on Dec. 24 and close on Jan. 5.

Recent findings suggest that in the window that ended on Jan. 5, 2026, the S&P 500 declined 0.11%, according to the Almanac. "Santa was a no-show for the third year in a row," the Almanac wrote. Before that, the S&P 500 also ended the Santa Claus rally windows of 2023 and 2024 lower.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delivery supply chains are the lifeblood of contemporary businesses — and a new startup is betting that purpose-built AI agents can make them run a lot more smoothly.

On Tuesday, Pedestal AI emerged from stealth with $4.7 million in seed funding. The company’s goal is to use agentic AI to make supply chains faster and more reliable — a initiative that’s already brought them together with Fortune 500 companies and some of the largest shipping firms in the world.

The seed round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage. Pedestal states the funding will be used to expand its product and engineering time, grow the marketing organization, and support additional deployments.

Sources indicate that in practice, much of Pedestal’s work is about removing friction from the shipping process — with agentic technology used as a means to that end. In one case, the organization reduced missed deliveries for a major furniture company by 20% by deploying agents to take on some of the work that drivers were supposed to do. The agentic system they built would call customers 30 minutes before a delivery and collect any special instructions; if the call didn’t go through, a text would be sent from a separate system. Along the way, the deployment collected a wealth of data about friction points in the process, which could be used to optimize the system even further.

Recent findings suggest that CEO Raj Aggarwal claims contemporary AI systems are particularly useful for dealing with that data. “The challenge is that the data is messy and it’s constantly changing,” Aggarwal told TechCrunch. “It’s disparate because it sits in so many legacy systems. That’s what makes it hard.”.

In a recent development, supply chain AI has become a particularly hot space in recent months as alumni from autonomous driving teams look to launch their own startups. The supply chain startup Atomic, released by a team of Tesla alumni, came out of stealth in 2025 with an emphasis on streamlining inventory. Another venture called Loop was launched by Uber alums to focus on predictive analytics.

According to recent reports, as Aggarwal sees it, deliveries are particularly well-suited to training reinforcement learning systems. Because of their high volumes and easily measured outcomes, it’s easy to fine-tune contemporary AI systems toward what’s working and away from what isn’t.

Perhaps most importantly, it’s the kind of problem that can have an immediate effect on a client’s bottom line, making it easy to justify the expense.

“If you can get it right,” he told TechCrunch, “you can have really big impact.”.
