📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a 2026 Gartner survey, 87% of customers noted companies using generative AI for customer service must provide access to a human agent.

That doesn’t mean customers are against AI. It means businesses need to think carefully about where they use it and where human support still matters.

Recent findings suggest that every business was built on a dream, and that’s a deeply human thing. When we replace real care with automation in the moments that matter most, we risk chipping away at the very thing that made the business worth building.

So how do you know where AI belongs and which moments need protecting? Start by asking four questions, then test your answers.

Before using AI in any area of your business, ask these four questions:.

Sources indicate that if a behind-the-scenes task is predictable, simple and low-stakes, let AI handle it. If it’s personal, complex or high-stakes, keep a person in the loop.

Industry observers note that I recently heard from an AnswerConnect client, Craig Grove, founder of GRT Realty, who learned the hard way where not to put AI. He partnered with an AI answering service, only to realize his leads were hanging up on the robot. After switching to human phone answering, he grew his business from six real estate agents to 70.

Running the four questions tells you where AI could go. Testing tells you whether it’s actually working.

According to recent reports, I’ve learned firsthand that even the best ideas benefit from a little testing before they’re rolled out more widely. I’m naturally someone who likes to take action, particularly when I’m confident something has potential. After a few instances where the direction or idea I had in mind wasn’t as great as I thought, I found myself in a place where I’d made mistakes.

It has been revealed that in hindsight, I should have started smaller, talked to more people and got feedback first. I’ve never regretted taking a little extra time to test an idea before jumping in. AI deserves the same approach.

Look at it from two angles: your customers and your team.

Then make testing a habit. Things are constantly changing, including your customers’ expectations. What worked in January can fail by June.

Industry observers note that AI is one of the most useful tools business owners have ever had. Used in the right place, it gives your people more time for the work that matters. Used in the wrong place, it erodes the trust your business was built on.

So ask the four questions, test the answers, and keep checking.

Your business was built on a dream. Use AI to help it grow, and keep people where your customers need them most.

  • Forty-six attorneys general have joined a New York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials revealed this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the company’s business practices.
  • Limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, softBank founder Masayoshi Son vowed tonight to “double down” on its investment in WeWork as he confirmed intends for a $9.5 billion rescue package that will provide up to $1.7 billion to WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann in exchange for cutting most ties with the manufacturer and will give SoftBank an 80 percent stake in the business. In a statement tonight in Upcoming York, SoftBank said it would “accelerate” WeWork’s path to profitability and positive free cash flow. More here in the Financial Times.

Forty-six attorneys general have joined a New York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials revealed this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the company’s business practices. The Washington Post has more here.

Limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted. VCs have begun knocking down their doors with requests for fresh capital commitments so they’ll have money to invest if the market cools down.

Industry observers note that the problem is, many of these LPs are already over-allocated. LPs traditionally invest in many asset classes, such as public equities, and they allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to venture capital. Suddenly, they’re finding they’ve forked over more than they’d intended to VCs.

Sources indicate that there are several reasons for this situation. First, VCs are returning to them ever faster for more capital  — sometimes in less than two years’ time  — because they are in vesting at such a furious pace.

Recent findings suggest that compounding the problem, not all LPs have received returns from their VC investments that they can recycle into latest venture capital allocations. In some cases, this capital is still tied up in startups that are raising much more money than in the past and staying private longer. “We have some large exposures to blue chip names where IPOs have been rumored to be coming for a long time already, and now it’s maybe 2021, maybe 2022,” states one manager who asked not to be named. In other cases where startups have gone public, falling prices have prompted VCs to hang on to their shares instead of distribute them.

The result is that LPs are having to cut back on the number of managers they can fund, and that could mean bad news for venture capitalists and startups alike. These LPs don’t have much choice. As the LP explains it, “We have a pretty structured allocation process, and we’re really trying to be creative,” she says. One venture manager who reappeared too rapidly for more money was  “easy to walk away from,” says this person. “Others, we’re having to do financial backflips for them to remain strong partners.” Either way, this LP adds, “We can’t add any latest relationships right now,” meaning new venture teams in particular are out of luck. “When [VCs] shorten their fundraising cycle by nine months to a year, you can only squeeze the balloon so much.”.

SoftBank’s $100 billion “Vision Fund” is one significant reason LPs find themselves in their current predicament. From the moment SoftBank began waving money around several years ago, it launched a vicious cycle. According to Chris Douvos, whose investment firm, Ahoy Capital, owns stakes in such venture funds as True Ventures and First Round Capital, “When Andreessen Horowitz hit the scene a decade ago, they changed the tempo of investing and everyone got more aggressive in their dealmaking as a response. Then SoftBank entered the picture in a big way, and it was like a16z on steroids.”.

Sources indicate that blueground, a six-year-old, Latest York-based startup providing turnkey flexible rental apartments, has raised $50 million in Series B funding, roughly six months after raising $20 million in Series A funding. WestCap Investment Partners and Prime Ventures co-led the round. More here.

According to recent reports, databricks, a six-year-old, San Francisco-based SaaS business that’s built on top of a bunch of open source tools, has raised a massive $400 million in Series F funding at a post-money valuation of $6.2 billion valuation. Today’s funding brings the total raised to almost a $900 million. Andreessen Horowitz led the round with latest investors BlackRock,  T. Rowe Price Associates, and Tiger Global Management also participating. TechCrunch has more here.

Sources indicate that ionQ, a four-year-old, College Park, Md.-based startup that uses charged particles suspended in a vacuum, as the basis for its hardware, has raised $55 million in funding. Samsung and Mubadala Capital co-led the round, joined by Amazon, GV, and Newly introduced Enterprise Associates. Fortune has more here.

In a recent development, aurora Insight, a three-year-old, Washington, D.C.-based startup that provides a “dynamic” global map of wireless connectivity that it built and monitors in real time using AI combined with data from sensors on satellites, vehicles, buildings, aircraft and other objects, has raised $18 million in Series A funding. Alsop Louie Partners and True Ventures co-led the round,  joined by Tippet Venture Partners, Rise of the Rest Seed Fund, Promus Ventures, Alumni Ventures Group, ValueStream Ventures, and Intellectus Partners. TechCrunch has more here.

Benevity, an 11-year-old, Calgary, Alberta-based company that makes corporate social responsibility and employee engagement software, has raised $30.5 million in Series C funding from General Atlantic and JMI Equity. More here. EV Connect, a 10-year-old, L.A.-based company that sells software to manage electric vehicle charging, has raised $12 million in a Series B round led by Mitsui & Co. and Ecosystem Integrity Fund. The company has raised $25 million to date. TechCrunch has more here.

Octave, a year-old, San Francisco-based tech-based behavioral health practice, has raised $11 million in Series A funding led by Greycroft, with participation from Obvious Ventures and earlier backers. The manufacturer has raised at least $14 million to date. Crunchbase News has more here.Signal AI, a six-year-old, London-based business intelligence and media monitoring startup, has raised $25 million in Series C funding. Redline Capital led the round, joined by MMC Ventures, GMG Ventures, and Hearst Ventures. TechCrunch has more here.

Recent findings suggest that allWork, a 3.5-year-old, New York-based on-demand work platform that’s targeting large enterprise customers in need of temporary workers, has raised $3.8 million in seed funding from Great Oaks, Lightspeed Scout Fund, The Fund, Fernbrook, SmartHub, and numerous angel investors. More here.

Sources indicate that beem, a year-old, Boston-based CBD organization that’s marketing its branded oils, protein bars, and a salve to athletes who may be looking for alternatives to chemically derived pain relievers and anti-inflammatories, has raised $5 million in seed funding led by Obvious Ventures. TechCrunch has more here.

Intrepida Bio, a newly launched, San Diego-based biotech focused on modulating innate immune systems, has raised $9.5 million from Sofinnova and Canaan Partners. FierceBiotech has more here.

It has been revealed that labGenius, a seven-year-old, London-based startup that’s applying AI and robotic automation to protein drug discovery, has raised $10 million in Series A funding. The round was led by Lux Capital and Obvious Ventures, with participation from Felicis Ventures, Inovia Capital, Air Street Capital and earlier investors, along with numerous notable individuals. TechCrunch has more here.

Margin Edge, a four-year-old, Falls Church, Va.-based maker of restaurant management software, has raised $5 million in Series A funding led by Osage Venture Partners, with participation from Good Tech giant. More here.

In a recent development, medinas, a two-year-old, Berkeley, Ca.-based company that helps healthcare organizations resell their surplus medical equipment and supplies, has raised $5 million in seed funding led by NFX. Additional investors in the round include Precursor Ventures, Sound Ventures, FJ Labs and Bryan Frist (of HCA Healthcare’s founding family). Crunchbase News has more here.

It has been revealed that mediView XR, a two-year-old, Cleveland, Oh.-based medical device organization working on a surgical navigation system that leverages augmented reality and spatial computing to provide surgeons with advanced visualization, has raised $4.5 million in seed funding. Backers include Inside View Investment,Plug and Play Ventures and Northwest Ohio Tech Fund. More here.

Reibus, a year-old, Atlanta, Ga.-based online marketplace for industrial materials, has raised $3.25 million in seed funding led by Bowery Capital, with participation from Initialized Capital and Stage 2 Capital. More here.

Industry observers note that marcelo Claure, the chief operating officer of SoftBank Group, will assume the position of executive chairman of the board of directors of WeWork when the tech giant receives a planned $1.5 billion payment from SoftBank. TechCrunch has more here.

John Donahoe, the current president and CEO of ServiceNow, is taking over as the CEO and president of Nike in January, replacing Mark Parker who has been since 2006 and lived through numerous controversies over the years. The company’s shareholders apparently prefer Donahoe, who is also the chairman of PayPal and a former CEO of eBay, which he led from 2008 through 2015. Zaz Floreani has joined the Austin-based venture firm Next Coast Ventures as a principal. Floreani was most recently the VP of corporate development at the same-day delivery organization Dropoff. More here.

Felicis leads $7.5M bet on Unsiloed AI to make enterprise documents usable by AI agents

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as businesses increasingly turn to AI agents to automate work, the vast amounts of information locked in complex documents remain a challenge.
  • Silicon Valley venture capital firm Felicis led the round, with participation from Y Combinator, Orange Collective, and Uncorrelated Ventures.
  • Business documents often include tables, charts, and complicated layouts that AI systems can struggle to interpret accurately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as businesses increasingly turn to AI agents to automate work, the vast amounts of information locked in complex documents remain a challenge. Unsiloed AI has raised $7.5 million in seed funding led by Felicis to tackle that problem, aiming to help enterprises make their documents more accessible to AI agents through specialized technology.

Silicon Valley venture capital firm Felicis led the round, with participation from Y Combinator, Orange Collective, and Uncorrelated Ventures. Angel investors Aarthi Ramamurthy and Beth Turner also participated.

Business documents often include tables, charts, and complicated layouts that AI systems can struggle to interpret accurately. But getting the information wrong can lead to costly mistakes for businesses, and the impact could be severe in the case of a bank, hospital, or a law firm, as they rely on these documents for their daily work.

According to recent reports, unsiloed aims to solve this problem with software that breaks down complex documents, extracts information from tables, charts, and other elements, and turns it into structured data that AI agents can use. The technology also indicates where the extracted information came from in the original document, so businesses can check the results rather than take the AI’s output at face value.

In a recent development, “The problem with LLMs is they’re inherently probabilistic,” noted Unsiloed co-founder and CEO Aman Mishra (pictured above, right) in an interview. “There is going to be some deviation induced. There is going to be some hallucination involved, and that has a massive negative impact downstream.”.

Sources indicate that mishra co-founded Unsiloed with Adnan Abbas (pictured above, left), his former classmate at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur. The two joined Y Combinator’s Fall 2025 batch after spending some time developing the technology.

Unsiloed is already working with customers in finance, legal services, and healthcare, Mishra told TechCrunch. One bank is using its technology to process documents, while a law firm has deployed it on its own servers to handle contracts and old case files, he noted, without naming either customer. Mishra, however, named voice AI startup Bolna AI as a customer, saying it uses Unsiloed to ingest knowledge bases for building voice agents.

Industry observers note that the San Francisco-headquartered startup has entered a market that is already crowded and includes specialized document-processing startups such as Reducto and Unstructured, as well as offerings from Microsoft and Amazon. Businesses also sometimes use general-purpose AI models to extract information from documents, giving Unsiloed another set of competitors.

Industry observers note that mishra told TechCrunch that Unsiloed’s advantage lies in how it processes complex documents. The startup uses what it calls “dual-stream” vision models, which handle text and image data separately, along with a technique called “heat map-based chunking” that helps identify the most notable parts of a document.

“In one of the streams you have the text tokens, in the other stream you have the exact image tokens,” Mishra stated. “This is something that we have spent a lot of time architecting.”.

The technology then directs more computing power toward areas such as figures, numbers, and charts. Unsiloed also uses a specialized decoder that takes industry-specific terminology into account, helping it distinguish between terms that can mean different things in different business contexts.

Supporting those claims, Mishra pointed to a test involving 542 financial documents supplied by an enterprise customer. Unsiloed achieved 99.78% accuracy across roughly 84,000 extracted data points, per a technical brief shared by the startup. The test compared Unsiloed with major AI models, Microsoft’s Azure Document Intelligence, and the customer’s in-house extraction tool. The results have, however, not been independently verified.

Unsiloed also claims to have outperformed competing AI document-processing tools on olmOCR-Bench, a public benchmark developed by Allen AI. In tests conducted by the startup, Unsiloed scored 88.0, compared with 66.0 for Reducto’s agentic system and 39.9 for Unstructured. The benchmark covered 1,403 PDF pages and tested how well the systems handled tables, mathematical expressions, scanned documents, and complex layouts.

It has been revealed that unsiloed’s pricing, Mishra said, starts at one cent per page. He asserted that the startup’s approach also helps keep its costs down by directing computing power toward the parts of a document that need the most attention, instead of processing every section in the same way.

It has been revealed that presently, Unsiloed has a headcount of seven people. The startup, Mishra mentioned, intends to use the fresh funding to hire more researchers and engineers, expand its sales efforts, and develop proprietary datasets to improve its technology.

#110494. Uncommon Thinkers: Saf Rabah wants to make it easier to build housing, one permit at a time

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1770 w)

Uncommon Thinkers: Saf Rabah wants to make it easier to build housing, one permit at a time

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1770 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Grace Kaste on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:50 amNovember 24, 2026 at 1:22 pm.
  • Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • When startup founder Safouen (Saf) Rabah decided to get in on the AI boom, he didn’t start by coding or by training any models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Grace Kaste on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:50 amNovember 24, 2026 at 1:22 pm.

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

When startup founder Safouen (Saf) Rabah decided to get in on the AI boom, he didn’t start by coding or by training any models. He got in touch with urban planners at Bellevue City Hall, and together they combed through nearly 300 land use permit applications to find common mistakes and bottlenecks.

Bellevue began using Rabah’s platform, Govstream.AI, in the summer of 2025, starting with an AI assistant for city staff. In a test using past applications, about three times as many were judged complete with Govstream’s tool. Rabah claims that change alone has the potential to alter the housing stock of the city.

“Why can’t we build more housing? All the macro economic reasons, inflation, material costs, labor, land scarcity, are all exacerbated by the slow permitting process,” Rabah mentioned. “That’s what we want to change.”.

So, how did Rabah, a B2B software engineer by training, find his way to land use permitting?

In a recent development, rabah hadn’t heard of the government technology sector, aka GovTech, until mid-career, but looking back, the signs were all there. He was born in Sfax, Tunisia, and grew up in Tunis. Throughout his childhood, he dreamed of running for office.

“I come from a small developing country, so there’s always this idea of, what could a small developing country become? How can it prosper and grow?” Rabah noted. “Building has always been a big part of what I imagined myself doing.”.

Industry observers note that as a teenager in the 1980s, he attended a USAID-funded boarding school in Tunis. The school was part of Cold War efforts to expand American soft power around the Middle East; classes were conducted in English and many of the students went on to university in North America.

“The school had the first Macintosh lab in all of Africa,” Rabah said. “I can still picture the USAID logo on the back of each computer.”.

Rabah got a scholarship to University of British Columbia, where he studied electrical engineering while running what he calls his “first entrepreneurial venture”: a service that built and hosted websites for small businesses.

That led to a job at a startup called Pivotal, a customer relationship management platform where Rabah led a team responsible for e-business applications. After Pivotal went public, Rabah left for a job at TELUS, one of Canada’s “big three” telecommunications corporations, but rapidly felt frustrated by the dynamics at such a large company.

“Even though I worked on nascent products, it was very, very bureaucratic,” Rabah said. “There were committees, a hundred thousand employees. I missed building things.”.

Rabah began to look for a upcoming job that would not only allow him to build but also to make a difference.

It has been revealed that “Being an immigrant, it’s always tempting to stay content with having a good job, good status,” Rabah said. “But I’ve always enjoyed the ‘what if?’ mindset, the clean slate. It’s this way today, but could we imagine it to be something different?”.

That vision led him to Socrata, which in 2010 was just a nascent government technology startup.

It has been revealed that “I really connected with the founder,” Rabah stated. “It had a really cool mission, it combined the ‘do-well’ with ‘do-good.’”.

Sources indicate that socrata was one of the first platforms to host data portals for local governments and federal agencies, allowing citizens to access and map public data sets. Many U.S. cities, including Seattle, still use Socrata’s software today to publish information including crime logs, permits, and budgets.

“We were a substantial part of pioneering the open data movement,” Rabah said. “At one point almost every major city was our customer, and half the states.”.

Socrata was acquired by Tyler Technologies in 2018, and Rabah stayed on until 2024.

“The funny part is today we use that data quite a lot in our work because one of the most popular data sets that any city publishes is its permit data,” Rabah said. “We’ve even built a connector between Socrata and Govstream.”.

But once Socrata was acquired, Rabah began to feel the same way he had at TELUS: boxed in by bureaucracy.

In a recent development, “Tyler was a really good company, but it is a major company,” Rabah said. “Tech was getting repetitive, and I was thinking about leaving it altogether.”.

“The thing that pushed me over the edge is that AI happened,” Rabah said. “It was one of those moments where once you start working with it, you really can’t help but think, ‘I can revisit virtually every assumption I’ve made over the last 20 years, every constraint.’”.

Immediately, he thought of his passion for building—building a startup, building a better country, and literally building a building.

Sources indicate that “I’ve been fascinated by the built environment since my Lego days: What makes some cities livable and others not?” Rabah said. “Then, living in Seattle, you see the lack of housing, affordability, and the homelessness problem we have, and you’re like, why can’t we build more housing? I started believing that these problems are in fact solvable if we simply speed things up and simplify things with AI.”.

In July of 2024, Rabah began working with his “design partner,” Bellevue’s Development Services Department, to learn more about common permitting problems.

It has been revealed that “We started with something visionary and high-level, but you can only get there if you understand the granular problems of the day-to-day,” Rabah mentioned. “So we talked with developers and builders and we talked with the people on the other side of the counter who are processing these permits and guiding these builders.”.

He learned that most permitting mistakes are avoidable, like applying for the wrong zone or forgetting to include a north arrow on an architectural plan. Those oversights can send an application back to square one while clogging up the permitting process for all other projects.

“The wait time disproportionately affects lower margin projects,” Rabah noted. “It really constrains the supply of housing, especially the housing we need more of, which is the more affordable kind.”.

According to recent reports, govstream’s AI assistants are designed to help first-time builders avoid those errors and make permitting faster for everyone. Rabah and his team began by building what they call an “intelligent intake” platform for a city permitting portal, which guided owners through preparing to submit their applications.

According to recent reports, when Bellevue first tested Govstream’s intake tool on 276 past residential building permit applications, the city reported a completeness rate of 67%, compared with 22% when those applications were originally filed. According to the company, the latest testing has yielded an 88% completeness rate.

More recently, they’ve begun to build out an AI assistant for the backend, which assists city permit techs with the initial review and reduces what Rabah calls “toil,” like answering unnecessary pre-application emails and tracking down missing documents.

Bellevue staff estimated that Govstream’s tools saved them 152 hours over one month this summer by helping them research and respond to pre-application inquiries.

“For a developer, time is money, so the type of housing that can be built in Bellevue will become more affordable,” remarked Jake Hesselgesser, Bellevue’s development services director. “This technology has a direct and material impact on the cost of housing.”.

Eventually, Govstream.AI will be an end-to-end service, assisting in later stages of the permitting process, too. But Rabah is emphatic that Govstream will not give AI the final say.

“We always put our AI systems in the role of assistants that suggest stuff, but never decide stuff,” Rabah noted.

Rabah says Govstream uses preset rules, outside the AI model, to check whether a portion of the application is complete, whether a site needs a geotechnical report, or whether an architect is properly licensed. In Bellevue, city staff retain final authority.

Hesselgesser remarked that Rabah’s conservative approach to AI is what made the city of Bellevue want to work with his startup.

Sources indicate that “Our core principle around Bellevue’s use of AI is to retain human decision making, and we wanted to ensure that we were aligned with a firm with the same core value,” Hesselgesser noted. “Saf took that holistic approach.”.

Recent findings suggest that around the office, Rabah has become known for his eagerness to build. According to Mariia Derevianko, head of marketing, he spends his weekends building out a product or an idea in order to workshop it with the team.

“He’s very hands-on with the product, with design, marketing, all of the aspects,” Derevianko said. “He never waits for the engineers to build something.”.

Most recently, he built a lead tracker to research which cities Govstream should partner with, and previously, he vibe-coded one of the research assistants in the Govstream platform as a template for his software engineers.

Derevianko, who joined the team last year after Rabah poached her from AWS, said he’s also known for his kindness.

In a recent development, “I originally didn’t want to join a start-up,” Derevianko said. “I only said yes because I saw he is a genuinely good person who really cares about this project.”.

Govstream.AI has already won at least 12 contracts around the Puget Sound, including King County and the City of Everett, as well as cities across the country, such as Louisville, Kentucky.

In a recent development, ultimately, Rabah has his eyes set on Seattle, where construction and development has been on the decline. Last December, the city council passed permanent “middle housing” rules to upzone residential neighborhoods and encourage the construction of ADUs, all of which will need a permit.

According to recent reports, seattle tested a competing AI tool from CivCheck in 2025. In June, city staff recommended a pilot that would let applicants check their submissions for completeness before filing.

According to recent reports, “We need affordable housing in Seattle,” Rabah said. “We would really, really love to help our home city streamline permitting and remove it as a barrier.”.

In founding Govstream.AI, Rabah has found the job he has been looking for: one in which he can build things without the bureaucracy of a large manufacturer, all while “doing good.”.

Industry observers note that “This has become my obsession,” Rabah said. “I can point to things in a city and say, maybe Govstream was a part of what allowed this project to get built.”.

Why This Analyst Isn’t Rushing to Buy XRP Below $1 Despite Predicting an Explosive Rally to $10

💡 Key Takeaways
  • XRP’s return below the psychologically notable $1 level hasn’t convinced every investor that it is time to buy the dip.
  • According to recent reports, in a November 19 post on X, crypto trader VirtualBacon identified the $1 price level as a potential bottoming zone for XRP in the current market cycle.
  • “For me, $1 is roughly the bottom area for this cycle,” he stated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

XRP’s return below the psychologically notable $1 level hasn’t convinced every investor that it is time to buy the dip. Despite believing the payments-based token could eventually climb to a staggering $10, one trader is holding back. His cautious stance raises an interesting question: if XRP has such massive upside potential, why is he waiting on the sidelines?

According to recent reports, in a November 19 post on X, crypto trader VirtualBacon identified the $1 price level as a potential bottoming zone for XRP in the current market cycle. The analyst suggested that the cryptocurrency may be approaching the lower end of its correction, even as selling pressure continues to weigh on its price.

“For me, $1 is roughly the bottom area for this cycle,” he stated.

While he described the $1 mark as the approximate bottoming zone for XRP during the ongoing cycle, he did not suggest that a definitive price floor had already been established.

His hesitation stems from the belief that investors will still have plenty of opportunities to accumulate alternative cryptocurrencies even after the broader market begins recovering. In his view, many altcoins could remain relatively cheap early in the next market rebound, meaning investors don’t necessarily need to rush into XRP before its downtrend runs its course.

“I’m not buying it yet,” he explained, making it clear that he would rather wait for a more favorable entry point than rush into the market.

XRP was trading at $0.9647 at the time of publication, down 2.3% over the previous 24 hours. The latest pullback followed a brief recovery to $1 on November 18, 2026, which proved short-lived as investors took profits, pushing the token back below the key psychological threshold.

Although VirtualBacon is not ready to accumulate XRP at current prices, he remains optimistic about its longer-term potential. The pundit believes the cryptocurrency could eventually reach $10, although he sees limited room for significant gains beyond that valuation.

It has been revealed that A rally to $10 would represent a major milestone for XRP, pushing its market capitalization to approximately $635 billion based on a circulating supply of 63.52 billion tokens. This would place the cryptocurrency among the largest digital assets by market value and require its valuation to grow more than tenfold from current levels.

The projected price target also highlights the scale of growth XRP would need. At $10 per token, its fully diluted valuation, calculated using the maximum supply of 100 billion XRP, would reach approximately $1 trillion.

However, reaching such a valuation would require sustained demand, increased market participation, and significant capital flowing into the cryptocurrency. Notably, while VirtualBacon considers $10 achievable over the longer term, his outlook suggests that he sees this level as a more realistic upper target rather than expecting XRP to deliver substantially higher gains.

Industry observers note that on Monday, XRP briefly rose above $1 after the return of Jensen Huang to Nvidia sparked a rally on Wall Street and a wave of short liquidations in the crypto market. At the peak of the move, short liquidations on XRP exceeded long liquidations by 578%, according to CoinGlass data.

On the XRPUSDT perpetual contract on Binance, the price of XRP went from $0.94 to as high as $1.02 within minutes after 14:00 UTC, and later it pulled back and stood at $0.984, according to TradingView.

Recent findings suggest that earlier on Monday, before the opening bell, Nvidia announced that its board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately. The company remarked that the board was satisfied with Huang's "candor and ability to lead" after a series of meetings with him, and that its independent investigation would continue. According to the company, the board received input from senior U.S. government officials and concluded that Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk.".

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones remarked in a statement.

Sources indicate that huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, and on Nov. 17, during the tech giant's earnings call, Jones said that the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.".

In premarket trading, Nvidia stock jumped 27% to $159.48 as of 9 a.m. ET, and at the start of U.S. trading on Monday, Nvidia shares were up more than 30%. The rally spread across Wall Street, and the S&P 500 rose as much as 5.6% and the Nasdaq 100 as much as 7.9%, according to NBC News.

CoinGlass data indicates that $9.45 million worth of XRP positions were liquidated over the past 24 hours, and $7.18 million of that amount came from short positions. Long positions accounted for $2.27 million.

Industry observers note that the same happened across the rest of the crypto market. In total, 110,663 traders were liquidated for $660.89 million over the past 24 hours, according to CoinGlass, and shorts accounted for $515.94 million of that amount.

It has been revealed that bitcoin led the list with $273.26 million in liquidations, and 82.8% of that amount came from short positions. Ethereum followed with $139.07 million, and Solana was third with $24.93 million.

Besides, perpetual contracts on Nvidia stock and on SOXL, a triple-leveraged exchange-traded fund on semiconductor stocks, were next on the list with $16.34 million and $15.01 million in liquidations, respectively, according to CoinGlass.

It has been revealed that this Saturday, November 28, is Small Business Saturday, the annual post-Thanksgiving tradition that urges holiday shoppers to buy from local, independent businesses. And Eva Longoria wants the people behind those businesses to feel supported all year long.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve always had so much respect for small business owners because I know firsthand what it takes to turn an idea into something real,” Longoria told Entrepreneur. “Being an entrepreneur can be incredibly rewarding, but it can also feel overwhelming when you’re making massive decisions and trying to figure things out on your own. That’s why I’m so passionate about supporting small businesses.”.

In a recent development, the actress, entrepreneur and investor has partnered with Lenovo on Backing Every Business, a global initiative released this year to close the support gap facing small businesses. Founders can apply for grant funding, AI-enabled technology and one-to-one mentorship, including from Longoria herself.

“No two small businesses face the same challenges, and the best support starts with listening,” Emily Ketchen, SVP and CMO of Intelligent Devices Group & International Markets at Lenovo, told Entrepreneur.

Sources indicate that at the heart of the initiative is Twinning, a mentorship program pairing small business owners across industries and borders. A fresh docuseries narrated by Longoria follows Twinning entrepreneurs as they tackle real business challenges together.

Industry observers note that and then there’s Call Eva, which gave entrepreneurs a direct line to Longoria, Lenovo’s global ambassador. Founders left voice notes with their biggest business questions, and select callers get to speak with her directly.

“It’s been rewarding to be part of something that helps small business owners feel supported as they grow,” Longoria added.

Industry observers note that the stakes are significant. The U.S. has 33.2 million small businesses that employ 61.6 million Americans and represent 43.5% of America’s GDP, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

It has been revealed that an analysis of 88 Call Eva submissions from eight countries revealed four overlapping themes. Here are the most common issues, and Longoria’s advice for overcoming them.

Industry observers note that 1. How to be seen. More than half asked about marketing and reaching new customers. Longoria’s advice: Lead with the story only your business can tell.

According to recent reports, “The tool that you have to use is storytelling,” she noted. “You’ve got to tell the story of the artisans and tell the story of the heritage behind these materials. I always think that cuts through the noise.”.

Sources indicate that 2. How to scale. Half asked about expanding without losing what makes them distinctive. Longoria urged starting focused and building on what works.

“I would think about one SKU, one target customer, one initial region, one retailer… Let’s see how that performs,” she mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that 3. How to lead and partner. One in five asked about juggling leadership and competing priorities. Longoria stressed finding collaborators whose audiences and values align.

“Who are they trying to reach? What’s their demographic? How do you make this a win for that brand?” she remarked.

It has been revealed that 4. How to fund the future. About one in eight asked about raising capital. Her advice: Find investors who bring expertise and relationships, not just cash.

“You’re looking for a partner that adds value and not just in money,” she remarked. “I think one of the biggest mistakes you can make is partnering with the wrong investor.”.

To see these lessons play out, watch the Backing Every Business Twinning docuseries on YouTube. Then, this Saturday, skip the big-box checkout line and support the shops, restaurants and makers in your neighborhood.

Breaking: 5 Interesting Startup Deals You May Have Missed: Reflecting Sunlight From Space, Better Breathing And Smarter Garbage Trucks

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar.
  • What if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth?
  • Those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar. Check out our previous entry here.

What if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth? Or researchers could send an experiment into space for less than the price of a car?

Those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month. Our latest roundup also includes a tech giant bringing AI to the old-school business of garbage hauling, another rethinking how factories are programmed, and a consumer brand betting that better breathing could become a big business. Let’s take a closer look.

Solar power has one rather obvious limitation: The sun goes down.

To that end, Reflect Orbital is working on a solution that sounds straight out of science fiction. The Hawthorne, California-based startup wants to put giant mirrors in orbit to redirect sunlight toward specific locations on Earth, potentially allowing solar farms to keep generating electricity longer after sunset.

Industry observers note that the firm recently confirmed $73.5 million in fresh funding, bringing its total funding to more than $102 million, per Crunchbase. Existing investors Sequoia Capital, Lux Capital and Starship Ventures participated, alongside new backers including Buckley Ventures, Convective Capital, The Uncommon Group and Salesforce Ventures 1.

Reflect Orbital is developing lightweight, foldable reflectors that it claims can be debuted aboard satellites and deployed in low Earth orbit. The firm envisions using them not only to extend solar power generation, but also to illuminate disaster zones for nighttime search-and-rescue operations or construction sites after dark.

The idea remains unproven in orbit, however. Reflect Orbital is targeting the second quarter of 2027 for its first demonstration mission, which has received FCC approval. The funding will help support those initial debuts, further development of its reflector technology, and commercial partnerships.

It has been revealed that the raise comes during a record year for space technology funding. By late August, investors had poured $20.3 billion into space- and satellite-related startups globally, per Crunchbase data, already comfortably exceeding previous annual records.

Nasal strips have been around for decades, but Intake Breathing Technology thinks there’s room for a serious upgrade.

The Santa Barbara, California-based consumer wellness company recently announced a $62 million investment from Camino Partners, the investment platform founded by KIND Snacks entrepreneur Daniel Lubetzky.

In a recent development, intake makes a patented magnetic nasal dilator designed to open nasal passages and improve airflow. Rather than relying on a conventional adhesive strip stretched across the nose, its system uses adhesive tabs and a reusable magnetic band to pull the sides of the nose outward.

The manufacturer markets its product to people looking to breathe more comfortably while sleeping, exercising or going about their daily routines. It claims it has sold more than 100 million pairs of breathing tabs since 2023, with triple-digit revenue growth over the past three years.

In a recent development, intake aims to use the new capital to expand beyond its direct-to-consumer business and into more mainstream retail channels. That’s where Lubetzky’s experience building KIND into a household name could prove useful.

Its funding comes as venture investors show renewed enthusiasm for fitness and wellness. Startups in those categories raised more than $3.6 billion globally in the first half of 2026, putting the sector on pace for its strongest funding year since 2022, Crunchbase data shows.

Industry observers note that interestingly, much of this year’s investment into the sector has flowed to wearable devices and health platforms built around AI and data. Intake is a somewhat different bet: a relatively simple physical product that has apparently found a sizable audience without promising to reinvent healthcare through software.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Fitness- And Wellness-Related Startup Funding In 2026.

According to recent reports, taking out the trash isn’t exactly rocket science. But managing the businesses that collect it turns out to be surprisingly complicated.

San Francisco-based TrashLab Software recently raised $12 million in a growth funding round led by Ventana, with participation from existing investors Bienville Capital, Harlem Capital and CreativeCo.

The startup builds an AI-powered operating platform for waste-hauling businesses, an industry where many smaller operators still rely on spreadsheets, paper routes and clunky software to manage their fleets.

Recent findings suggest that trashLab says its platform combines dispatching, route planning, customer management, billing and payments. Its AI agent, called Haul-E, can answer customer calls and take orders, while cameras in garbage trucks can help document problems such as overflowing dumpsters, blocked containers or bins that weren’t put out for collection.

Recent findings suggest that the organization states hundreds of waste haulers across the U.S. and Canada now use its software, and that more than 5 million tons of material have been managed through its platform.

It’s not the only startup finding an AI opportunity in the waste industry. We recently covered Greyparrot, a London-based company using computer vision to identify and analyze waste moving through recycling facilities. While Greyparrot focuses on what happens after trash reaches a processing plant, TrashLab is tackling the messy logistics of getting it there.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Venture Funding To Waste Management Startups In 2026.

Factory automation has come a long way, but programming the machines that run industrial production lines can still require specialized expertise and a lot of time.

Gardena, California-based Neuron Industries wants to make the process a lot simpler.

The startup recently confirmed a $10 million seed round co-led by FCVC and Obvious Ventures, with participation from Y Combinator, Thin Line Capital, Zee Prime Capital and Founder Factor.

Neuron is developing a new kind of industrial controller — the hardware that coordinates sensors, motors and other equipment in factories — alongside AI-powered software that lets engineers describe what they want a machine to do in ordinary language.

According to recent reports, its system generates control code that engineers can inspect, modify and test in simulation before deploying it to real equipment. The goal is to reduce the time and specialized programming knowledge needed to get new production lines up and running.

The startup indicates it has already demonstrated its technology on existing factory equipment, including replacing an aging controller on a wood-processing line with roughly three hours of engineering work and eight hours of downtime. It intends to release its Cortex AI Controller commercially in early 2027.

According to recent reports, the investment fits into a broader surge in funding for physical AI — technology that applies artificial intelligence to robots, autonomous vehicles, industrial equipment and other machines in the real world. Startups in those categories raised $47.4 billion globally across 521 deals in the first half of 2026, nearly 4x the amount invested in the second half of 2025, according to Crunchbase data.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Physical AI Venture Funding In 2026.

Sending an experiment into space has traditionally required years of preparation, specialized engineering expertise and a very substantial budget.

Austria-based Tumbleweed wants to bring the cost of entry down to as little as 15,000 euros.

Sources indicate that the Vienna startup recently raised 6.9 million euros (roughly $8 million) in seed funding led by PactVC, with participation from Vanagon Ventures, Prototype Capital and EWOR, among other investors. The company describes it as the largest space-tech seed round raised in Austria to date.

Tumbleweed develops standardized containers, called Pods, that allow researchers and companies to conduct experiments in microgravity without building their own satellites or navigating the complex certification process required for space missions.

Industry observers note that customers can place their experiments inside the pre-certified containers, which provide power and communications capabilities while in orbit. The startup handles the logistics of launching the payloads and transmitting experimental data back to Earth.

Unlike many space startups still working toward their first launch, Tumbleweed has already put hardware in orbit. Its inaugural Oasis Alpha satellite rolled out in July carrying experiments for four paying customers, including research into biological processes and space-resource technologies. The mission was fully booked a year before launch.

Tumbleweed notes its new funding will help it carry out three more missions in 2027 and develop a next-generation spacecraft that would allow customers to bring physical samples back to Earth beginning in 2028.

In a recent development, tumbleweed is part of a growing European space startup ecosystem, although funding remains concentrated elsewhere. As of late August, European companies had attracted about 10% of global space-tech venture investment in 2026, compared with the more than 60% going to U.S. startups, Crunchbase data shows.

Related Crunchbase query: Space And Satellite Tech Startup Funding.

As the report notes: “SoftBank won approval from the panel to buy Sprint Corp. and U.K. chip designer ARM Holdings. However, the committee put conditions on its ownership of Sprint, and restricted its control of alternative-asset manager Fortress Investment Group. More recently, SoftBank was unable to fill two board seats at one of its portfolio companies, Uber Technologies, because it did not have Cfius approval.”.

According to recent reports, tesla delivered a strong third-quarter earnings report after the bell today, posting a surprise profit and telling shareholders it’s ahead of schedule with a upcoming factory in Shanghai. Shares rose more than 20 percent after hours. CNBC has more here.

A couple of years ago, the cofounder and CEO of a blood-testing firm was publicly taken to task for implying in articles and professional profiles that he has a PhD when in reality, he’d left a prestigious graduate group three years after enrolling, without a degree.

The CEO is hardly alone in intentionally or otherwise sowing confusion around his credentials, however. Over the years, we’ve mistakenly believed that a number of founders have obtained specific college degrees based on their LinkedIn bio, only to learn offline that they enrolled for some period of time in a particular program that they didn’t complete.

It happened most recently with the cofounder of a startup who one would might surmise based on his LinkedIn profile has a master’s degree from Harvard but does not. We also misunderstood the CEO of a robotics manufacturer to have a PhD based on her LinkedIn. It was our fault; it mentioned under the credit that she’d left to start a company. But anyone scanning the site might have come to the same wrong conclusion. (We pointed this out to her team, and mention of the PhD was deleted.).

In a higher-profile case, James Damore, the fired Google engineer who authored that infamous memo about the organization’s diversity practices and whose LinkedIn page cited under “Education” a “PhD, Systems Biology,” removed mention of those doctoral studies after Wired confirmed with Harvard that he was enrolled in the program but didn’t complete the doctorate.

Damore tried to defend his own LinkedIn profile, tweeting at the time, “I never told anyone I have a PhD. LinkedIn can’t distinguish between being in the PhD program and having a PhD (I forgot to update it).”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Zin Boats made a splash with fast, pricey electric boats.
  • The Seattle startup has launched Zin Power, a upcoming division that will supply its electric propulsion systems to other boat builders and to industries that rely on diesel engines, such as construction and mining.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:58 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:58 am.

Zin Boats made a splash with fast, pricey electric boats. But most of its business is now coming from what’s under the floor.

The Seattle startup has launched Zin Power, a upcoming division that will supply its electric propulsion systems to other boat builders and to industries that rely on diesel engines, such as construction and mining.

The company also raised $5 million to scale up production and expanded its headquarters in the Interbay neighborhood to 11,000 square feet.

It has been revealed that about 90% of the company’s revenue comes from selling motors and batteries to customers in the marine and drone industries, founder and CEO Piotr Zin told GeekWire. A typical setup includes two motors and about 500 kilowatt-hours of battery storage.

“We noticed a steady demand for pleasure craft year over year, but at the same time a massive increase in propulsion sales,” Zin said.

Customers include StanCraft Wooden Boats, which teamed with Zin on the 340 Hammerhead E, an all-electric wooden runabout. StanCraft delivered the first one to a customer this summer.

GeekWire first checked out the tech giant in early 2024, when it was relaunching after a pandemic shutdown with its Z2R, a 20-foot carbon fiber runabout. Later that year Zin indicated off the Z11, a 37-foot electric tender designed to shuttle passengers to and from megayachts at more than 60 mph. The company stated boats on the platform would cost $1.75 million to $3.75 million.

Sources indicate that the company also offers the Z7 Convertible, a 22-foot runabout with a removable roof that it pitches for fishing, surfing and cruising. The boat has a top speed of 40 mph and a range of more than 80 miles.

Zin Power grew out of the drivetrains engineered for those boats. Zin sees the marine track record as a selling point for other industries that need high torque, including construction, mining and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs).

“The ocean is one of the harshest environments there is, so the technology has already proven itself under about the toughest conditions it could face,” Zin stated.

Many of those machines still run on diesel engines, a technology more than a century old. Zin mentioned operators are eager to switch to electric.

“What’s interesting is that economics is driving the shift, not regulation or image,” he remarked.

Electric systems cost up to 70% less to operate, according to Zin. He estimated that replacing a single 250-horsepower industrial diesel engine that runs eight hours a day could save as much as $1.5 million over 10 years.

It has been revealed that the latest funding will pay for more manufacturing capacity, a dedicated sales and engineering team to work with boat builders, and support for customers converting from diesel. Zin calls it a seed round, with a larger raise planned down the road. The company has raised $6.5 million to date, including a $1.275 million seed round in early 2024.

Zin Boats has nine full-time employees and brings on about a dozen contractors as needed.

In a recent development, for now, each Zin Power system is built to order. The company’s motors range from 100 to 600 kilowatts and deliver up to 2,700 pound-feet of torque, and its systems can run fully electric or as hybrids. A proprietary control unit that Zin Power calls the “Magic Box” manages everything from charging and cooling to software and safety.

“Our goal is to keep delivering what we’ve built while developing simpler, more advanced plug-and-play systems,” Zin mentioned. “Eventually, we want a customer to be able to pull out a diesel engine and drop in a Zin Power system as a direct one-for-one replacement.”.

Industry News: FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1597 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that finCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange.
  • Recent findings suggest that MEXC claims user assets remain secure.
  • On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that finCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange. The order spells out what is banned, what MEXC is accused of, and how the exchange has answered.

Recent findings suggest that MEXC claims user assets remain secure. The FinCEN order never suggested otherwise, and the gap between the exchange's reassurance and the order's actual target is the key to this story.

On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. It names MEXC Global a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance. From there, it bars "covered financial institutions," a category that includes banks, broker-dealers and money transmitters, from any transmittal of funds to or from MEXC Global. Transmittals, as defined, include convertible virtual currency.

On the MEXC side, the reach is wide. The order covers the exchange's subsidiaries, branches and offices outside the United States: MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles, MEXC Estonia OÜ, GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland and MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom. Former Singapore entities and any successors are included as well. US-based affiliates, by contrast, are expressly excluded.

The ban won't bite right away. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of the announcement, and it carries no end date. FinCEN keeps the authority to attach conditions and grant exemptions, and willful violations can lead to civil and criminal penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322.

MEXC's statement is short and carefully built. The exchange indicates it is aware of the order and is reviewing it with its legal and compliance teams. It describes itself as operating normally, with user assets secure. It also says it takes the concerns seriously, aims to engage constructively with FinCEN and other regulators, and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

Two points stand out. For one, the reassurance lines up with the order's text. Nothing in it freezes balances or halts trading, so "operating normally" is plausible. The threat is to MEXC's access to US financial counterparties, not to the exchange's wallets.

In a recent development, the other point is what the statement skips. It disputes none of the allegations, and the independent review it promises targets AML and sanctions controls, the very area where FinCEN says the exchange failed. The order also invites anyone with relevant information to submit it to FinCEN, so MEXC already has a formal channel for the constructive engagement it describes.

The charges are specific. FinCEN assesses that MEXC facilitated at least $16.7 billion in likely illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, a figure Treasury's announcement rounded to $16 billion. The order splits that total across several categories.

According to recent reports, on Russia, FinCEN cites nearly $1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to sanctions-evasion transactions, including $232 million in direct dealings with entities sanctioned by the US, EU or UK. According to the order, MEXC processed about $129 million with Garantex and $4.1 million with its successor Grinex after both were designated, with activity continuing as recently as June 2026. It also points to at least $26 million benefiting the A7 Network and nearly $200 million tied to the ruble-backed A7A5 token. Beyond that, FinCEN states MEXC handled more than $13 billion with four UK-sanctioned exchanges between May 2018 and July 2026.

In a recent development, iran features just as heavily. The order cites nearly $2 billion tied to Iranian actors or terrorist groups, including about $1.87 billion in exposure to Iran and over $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 Iranian exchanges. About $22 million is linked to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC Quds Force. For North Korea, the order describes roughly $350,000 received by a sanctioned money launderer between June and September 2025. On cybercrime, it cites $1.99 billion in flows linked to illicit cyber actors and $37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments between January 2022 and July 2024.

Industry observers note that the order then turns to MEXC's own rulebook. Its stated KYC and AML policies prohibit accounts in certain jurisdictions, yet FinCEN notes the exchange facilitated transactions involving them. The order also notes that MEXC has operated without a license in Seychelles, Hong Kong and Japan, and it points to the Seychelles Financial Services Authority's May 2026 enforcement action against MX Global Ltd. All of this reflects FinCEN's assessments, drawn from public and non-public information, and MEXC has not answered them point by point.

It has been revealed that the order is not an OFAC sanctions designation, and the difference matters. A funds-transmittal ban limits what US-covered institutions can do with MEXC. It does not make it illegal for ordinary consumers anywhere in the world to hold an account there. The order also states that it leaves existing Bank Secrecy Act and OFAC obligations untouched.

Section 9714 gives Treasury two routes: the special measures of Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, or a ban on certain transmittals of funds. FinCEN took the second and explained its reasoning. Recordkeeping requirements would still let transfers continue, and a correspondent-account restriction would miss funds moving outside a strict correspondent relationship. FinCEN also went with an order rather than a rulemaking, citing imminent threats and ongoing transactions.

One provision stands out for its practicality. FinCEN acknowledges that a covered institution often can't reject incoming crypto before it arrives, so the order allows discretion in cases such as funds that sat in an unhosted wallet for an extended period. The carve-out underlines how difficult enforcement will be in practice.

For most MEXC customers outside the US, nothing changes on day one. Counterparties face a tougher picture. Once the order takes effect, US banks, regulated exchanges and money transmitters will have to block transmittals to and from MEXC, and global institutions with US exposure have strong reasons to follow suit. FinCEN claims plainly that the order puts US and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice.

Industry observers note that before issuance, the draft went to the Justice Department, State, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the SEC, the CFTC, the OCC and the NCUA, and none objected. The order also fits into a wider Treasury campaign. It cites the October 1 Operation Economic Outcast action against the A7 Network, and a separate FinCEN proposal on A7 sub-agents followed days later.

According to recent reports, predicting how consumers or markets will react would be guesswork. What users can do is track the dates, know which institutions they depend on, and watch for official updates from MEXC.

Industry observers note that finCEN used the same Section 9714 authority against the exchange Bitzlato in January 2023. This time, though, the target is by FinCEN's own account among the 20 largest exchanges by trading volume, with roughly 9% of centralized exchange market share as of December 2025 and about $5 billion in reserve assets as of June 2026. Applying a transmittal ban to an exchange of that size signals a more aggressive posture.

It has been revealed that three things will show what comes next. The first is the Federal Register publication date, which starts the 30-day clock. The second is whether FinCEN grants any exemptions or conditions. The third is what MEXC's independent review turns up, and whether the exchange shares the results. For now, the statement buys MEXC time without answering the order. The real answer will come from changes to its controls, and from whether its banking and liquidity partners are satisfied with them.

U.K.-based fintech Payhawk declared a $280 million Series C funding round Wednesday, led by Goldman Sachs’ growth equity arm, making it one of Europe’s largest Series C rounds this year, as noted by Sifted. The round values the company at $2 billion, bringing its total funding to more than $500 million to date.

Founded in 2018, Payhawk is an enterprise financial management platform that helps companies track and manage expenses and procurement using AI agents. Speaking to FinTech magazine, Payhawk’s co-founder and CEO, Hristo Borisov, mentioned the company saw “an incredible growth opportunity and room to bring finance teams AI-native products that combine agents, payment infrastructure, and enterprise controls.”.

Payhawk competes with spend management companies Pleo, Moss, and Spendesk, and notes it operates in 33 countries. Notably, the tech giant stated it still has 70% of the $100 million it raised in 2022, a round that valued the company at $1 billion. This fresh capital will support its global expansion. Other investors in the round include Greenoaks, Lightspeed, and QED.

The United States Department of Justice (DOJ) has initiated a significant legal push to address the theft of over $6 billion worth of cryptocurrency from Binance by North Korean hackers last month.

Industry observers note that as per a Nov. 23 announcement, the DOJ mentioned that it has filed a civil forfeiture complaint to recover over $1.1 billion worth of stolen cryptocurrency as part of its efforts to retrieve the billions lost in the massive hack.

Industry observers note that the recent development comes less than a month after North Korean hackers reportedly broke into Binance on Oct. 29 in one of the biggest crypto heists ever.

The DOJ claimed that its recent civil forfeiture action focuses on over $1.1 billion worth of USD Coin (USDC), a stablecoin pegged 1:1 to the U.S. dollar and issued by Circle.

The assets are alleged to have been stolen from Binance and laundered by North Korean cybercriminals.

It has been revealed that significantly, the assets had previously been frozen under a restraining order obtained by the government earlier this month. With the fresh court filing, the potential recovery of the assets has taken another step forward.

According to recent reports, the DOJ further claimed that U.S. authorities have successfully helped freeze, seize or return over $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency since the attack in October.

This is nearly half of the total $6 billion-plus stolen from Binance, though the government did not provide details about how much of that has been returned to the exchange.

The importance of collaboration between law enforcement agencies and crypto firms to ensure that hackers don't get away with stolen assets was stressed by Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva.

“North Korean cyber hackers stole over $6 billion of cryptocurrency from Binance. But prompt coordination with both the government and our private sector partners helped to avoid the bulk of these assets from being lost,” Duva mentioned.

U.S. authorities have further revealed the sophisticated money laundering techniques used by North Korean hackers to conceal their stolen cryptocurrency.

FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said that the regime uses intricate money laundering methods to convert stolen digital assets into funds for its illicit activities.

After the Binance hack, authorities promptly worked to trace the stolen funds and coordinate with crypto service providers to block further transfers.

Sources indicate that the U.S. Secret Service claimed that its investigators were able to detect and freeze some of the stolen funds within minutes of the hack.

"The bad actors in this intrusion thought they could run from law enforcement. They've found out they were wrong," noted Secret Service Special Agent in Charge Todd Bratz.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recent findings suggest that A large company had finished moving a group of business customers onto a newly introduced billing platform. The implementation team completed migration testing, reconciled the account data and handed the platform to billing operations, which would run the process day to day.

According to recent reports, operations accepted the migrated accounts, the required defects were closed, and the implementation work moved to “complete” status. The project team then shifted to the next group of customers.

Sources indicate that three weeks later, billing specialists began finding a recurring problem in a small set of migrated accounts. The records matched the approved migration rules, but certain combinations of account settings forced specialists to correct fields manually before an invoice could be released.

Each correction was manageable, but the pattern became expensive only after the same work kept appearing in normal billing activity.

The difference became clearer at the next billing cycle.

Sources indicate that the affected accounts didn’t fail in the same way every time. One required a manual tax treatment, another needed a contract setting corrected, and another triggered an exception only after a billing adjustment.

Industry observers note that each case looked like “ordinary operating cleanup” until the team compared them and found the migration pattern underneath. That comparison took time because the work was being recorded where it occurred.

None of those activities were recorded as a reopened implementation concern while the project remained closed.

According to recent reports, the cost highlighted up first in operating time. Billing specialists who should have been reviewing current invoices were opening migrated accounts, comparing settings and correcting fields before invoices could move.

In a recent development, team leads added exception checks to the billing cycle, and finance partners joined troubleshooting calls to understand why the same account pattern kept reappearing. Customer-service teams then had to answer questions when invoice timing slipped for affected accounts.

The extra work sat inside operations. It didn’t reopen the implementation project, and it didn’t change the completion status already recorded for the migration.

According to recent reports, the billing team also had to protect normal work while dealing with the exceptions. Meanwhile, experienced specialists spent part of each cycle correcting migrated accounts, which left less time for current billing concerns that had nothing to do with the migration.

In a recent development, as the pattern continued, managers started moving work between people to keep invoices flowing. The platform had been delivered, but the receiving team was now carrying a recurring cost that hadn’t existed before the change.

Recent findings suggest that this is where the “Broken Handoffs” execution leak appears. The receiving team got the system, the documentation and the agreed support path, and the handoff itself worked as designed.

Industry observers note that those measures answered different questions. One captured whether the agreed work crossed the boundary successfully, while the other captured what it took to make that work function after the boundary.

It has been revealed that once the project closed, the operating cost had no direct route back into the measure that had already recorded the implementation as complete. The consequence stayed visible, but it lived in a different record.

In a recent development, the sensible response was to strengthen acceptance before the next group of customers. The company did three things:.

Those changes helped. More configuration problems were caught before transfer, and operations had a stronger basis for accepting the work.

The acceptance test still judged the deliverable at the moment of handoff. The recurring manual effort only became visible after enough migrated accounts passed through normal billing for the pattern to emerge.

A stronger test can reduce what crosses the boundary, but it still closes the project before downstream work has had time to reveal every consequence.

It has been revealed that for the next group of customers, the stronger checks caught several configuration issues before transfer. Operations accepted the migrated accounts, the implementation work closed, and billing moved into the normal cycle with fewer exceptions than before.

A different pattern surfaced later.

A subset of accounts required manual correction only after a billing adjustment changed how two fields interacted. The migration had passed the stronger acceptance test because the issue didn’t appear until those accounts went through live billing activity.

Recent findings suggest that billing specialists again became the first people to see the consequence. They reopened affected accounts, compared the fresh exceptions with the earlier corrections and traced which cases required manual handling before invoices could move.

The implementation record still demonstrated a “completed migration” while the added work accumulated inside the billing cycle.

The organization also kept the implementation team available during a stabilization period. That gave operations a route back when the account pattern became clear.

Support path? It worked, and specialists traced the configuration logic, changed the migration rule for the next group of customers and helped operations clean up the affected accounts.

Recent findings suggest that the technical issue was fixed; however, the earlier operating cost remained where it had been counted. Billing had already spent time on corrections, finance had already absorbed additional review work, and customer service had already handled the questions created by delayed invoices.

Post-launch support corrected the problem after transfer, but it didn’t change the fact that the implementation had already been recorded as complete before the cost appeared.

According to recent reports, A finished project can keep generating work after its own measures say the work is over. The receiving team carries the effect in operating time, service activity or rework while the sending team’s completion record remains unchanged.

Industry observers note that A pattern like this becomes especially hard to see when both records are accurate. An implementation team can show that the agreed migration work passed its tests and was accepted. Operations can show that the live process now requires additional effort.

No one has to misreport anything. The separation sits in where each result is counted.

That’s why the mechanism survives good project management, stronger acceptance and responsive support. The organization has improved how work crosses the boundary without reconnecting where completion is counted to where the later consequence appears.

A project isn’t finished when the work closes in one system while the cost of making it work continues to accumulate in another.
