Shiba Inu (SHIB) community members have launched a new block explorer for Shibarium, the layer-2 network of the SHIB ecosystem, and Shiba Inu lead Shytoshi Kusama has remained silent on X since May.

Shiba Inu community veteran Mazrael confirmed the new explorer, scan.shibfun.app, in an X post. "Shibarium has a new block explorer," he wrote. According to Mazrael, the explorer was "built by the community, powered by ShibWatch, dressed in the Eternity Hub look.".

The launch comes as SHIB trades near its lowest levels in years. In November, the price of SHIB fell as low as $0.00000337, its lowest level since 2021, and on Nov. 22, the token traded at around $0.00000362, according to CoinMarketCap.

Recent findings suggest that according to the post, users can type a .shib name in the search bar and land on the wallet linked to it, and the explorer also highlights new Shiboshis from Shibarium every day. For developers, Mazrael listed contract verification, read and write functions for contracts, the activity of ERC-4337 smart wallets, and a free API, which he described as "Etherscan-style too." Method names are decoded as well, and in Mazrael's words, there are "no more mystery 0x codes." The explorer also has a DApps page with Shibarium games and apps, and a button that adds Shibarium to a wallet in one click.

The work on the explorer is not finished yet. "Live blocks are complete now, and older history indexing," Mazrael wrote. On Tuesday, the explorer itself showed that 3% of Shibarium blocks had been indexed, and a notice on the site noted that some of the counts may be inaccurate. Mazrael added that the fresh explorer can be found on Shib.io under ShibWatch.

It has been revealed that shytoshi Kusama's last post or interaction on X dates back to May 13, 2026. In September, Kusama changed his X bio to "Polish" and his location to "Close," and he has not explained the meaning of either word. The official Shibarium account on X has not posted since July 13, 2026.

Still, Shibarium updates kept coming from community members. In October, Mazrael stated that CreateX, a standard factory for deploying contracts at the same address on different chains, went live on Shibarium. According to Mazrael, all 12 Safe v1.4.1 contracts were deployed to their canonical addresses through the Safe Singleton Factory, and x402 went live too, so AI agents can now pay in SHIB, TREAT and wrapped BONE.

In September 2025, attackers exploited the Shibarium bridge and withdrew about $2.4 million worth of assets from it.

According to recent reports, according to Shibariumscan, Shibarium processed 546 transactions in a single day in late November, and on Oct. 31, the daily number of transactions on the network was 6,370. Since its launch in August 2023, Shibarium has processed more than 1.5 billion transactions in total.

At the same time, the number of SHIB holders on Ethereum passed 1.7 million on Nov. 17, according to Etherscan.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.

In a recent development, the U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.

Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion, the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.

In a recent development, pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in Fresh Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size, Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.

Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.

Sources indicate that like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.

Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption.

Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.

Industry observers note that “My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website. “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that chan Park feels like “an eternal nomad.” He has since age 12, when he moved from Korea to the U.S., where he attended middle school in Minnesota, followed by high school in Newly introduced Jersey, followed by college in New Hampshire. Then he really began to bounce around. Park worked as a trader in New York out of college, embraced the ski-bum life in Utah, then headed to Asia for Uber, where he spent six years, running its expansion team, then managing its entire Southeast Asia business out of Singapore.

More specifically, he was responsible for eight countries across the region, and 350 people, which didn’t give him a lot of time to organize his home. But he wasn’t overwhelmed by the chaos. Instead, he says that in Singapore, something unusual happened. “There’s this huge culture of landlords furnishing space to attract expats,” explains Park. “The furnishings aren’t super high-end, but they’re well-designed and well put together, and it enabled me to be basically moved in as soon as I put my clothes in the closet.” Suddenly, coming home was a treat — a new sensation for him. “For the first time, I was proud to host friends for dinners and barbecues and to just open the door and relax.”.

In a recent development, park knew his U.S. friends could benefit from the same experience, and before long, he was talking with his Dartmouth classmate turned product and industrial designer Christian Talmage about forming their own organization. Enter Oliver Space, which provides a lot of what that Singaporean landlord delivered to Park. It furnishes places for busy professionals, making moving into a upcoming home as easy as hanging up their clothes.

According to recent reports, the now year-old service is available in the Bay Area only. And Oliver Space employs just a dozen people so far. But the firm has already gained enough traction to attract $6.8 million in seed funding from an interesting array of investors, including Mayfield, Abstract Ventures, investors Jana Messerschmidt and April Underwood, Opendoor founder Eric Wu, and Kevin and Julia Hartz of Eventbrite, among others.

Now, Oliver Space just has to grow as promptly, or more so, than other furniture-as-service startups to recently attract funding.

AI Bias In HR: Why Polished Work Gets Overrated And What to Do About It

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in today’s world, all professional employees use AI, whether it’s candidates submitting highly polished CVs with 100% perfect fit with your job description to AI-generated work.
  • Imagine this: You’re hiring a financial analyst and give two finalists the same AI-generated acquisition memo.
  • According to recent reports, one candidate improves the slides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in today’s world, all professional employees use AI, whether it’s candidates submitting highly polished CVs with 100% perfect fit with your job description to AI-generated work. In this environment, how can we promote the right employees and how do we hire the best canidates when everyone appears to be perfect?

Imagine this: You’re hiring a financial analyst and give two finalists the same AI-generated acquisition memo. It reads beautifully and recommends buying a company at what looks like a reasonable price. There’s one problem. The model counted the same revenue twice.

According to recent reports, one candidate improves the slides. The other asks for the source data, spots the error and changes the recommendation. If I’d asked for a polished take-home assignment and used AI to grade it, I might have hired the better slide editor.

AI has become a significant part of how people apply for jobs and how they do that work. Using AI to police that behavior is a losing game. Employers have more to gain by making AI use visible and designing hiring and performance reviews around what people do with it.

It has been revealed that indeed illustrates both sides of the hiring loop. Its Career Scout offers job seekers résumé help, while its employer tools help review applications against hiring criteria. Both can save time, and résumé assistance can help a qualified applicant explain experience they’ve struggled to put into words.

But it can also make two very different candidates look equally well-suited for a role on paper.

An AI detector adds another score without answering the question the employer cares about: Could this person do the job?

Sources indicate that I’d use AI to help the recruiter prepare a better follow-up. If someone says they led an integration, ask them to walk through a decision they made when two teams disagreed. The résumé gets you to the question. The answer gives you something to evaluate.

In a recent development, coderPad offers an interview environment where candidates use AI on realistic tasks while interviewers watch how they prompt, evaluate and revise the output. That gives employers a practical way to observe a skill candidates will increasingly need on the job.

I’d give every finalist the same flawed acquisition memo, the same source documents and access to the same AI tools. Then I’d ask what they would verify before sending the memo to a client. One might catch the double-counted revenue. Another might go further and work out whether the corrected numbers change the price we should offer. The most revealing moment may come when the tool confidently insists its original calculation was right. What does the candidate do then?

According to recent reports, lattice lets managers use AI to draft reviews from goals, feedback and meeting notes. Synq, formerly Gloat, indicates its software can build and run a review cycle from a plain-English instruction. These tools make it easier to collect and summarize evidence. That makes the choice of what to collect more consequential.

#110456. Nanbeige4.3-33B Ties Qwen3.8-27B on Intelligence Index, but Spends 44% More Output Tokens

📖 Baca

Nanbeige4.3-33B Ties Qwen3.8-27B on Intelligence Index, but Spends 44% More Output Tokens

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1100 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K.
  • Two models just posted the same score.
  • Recent findings suggest that nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K. Here is what that costs locally.

Two models just posted the same score. One needed 158,000 output tokens per task to get there. The other needed 110,000.

Recent findings suggest that nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5. According to Artificial Analysis's evaluation, published November 5, that matches Qwen3.8 27B at its xhigh reasoning setting. The model is open weights under Apache 2.0, accepts text only, and has a 524K-token context window.

According to recent reports, behind the tie sits a gap in effort. Artificial Analysis says Nanbeige used 158K output tokens per Intelligence Index task against 110K for Qwen3.8 27B, about 44% more. That weighted average covers answer and reasoning tokens across all nine v5 evaluations, including agentic tool-use turns. For anyone running these models, tokens translate into time, electricity or money, so the same score doesn't mean the same cost.

Sources indicate that the Intelligence Index v5 combines nine evaluations, among them AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode 2.0 and AA-Omniscience. A score of 20 puts Nanbeige well above the 6 of Muse Glimmer, a 30B model in the same comparison. Artificial Analysis also notes that Nanbeige sets a new Pareto-optimal point for Intelligence Index against total parameters, since both it and Qwen3.8 27B are dense models. A larger mixture-of-experts model like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, by contrast, scores 33 while activating only 16B parameters per token.

The model card Nanbeige's lab published on Hugging Face describes the base model, positioned as the flagship teacher for the Nanbeige4.3 series. The lab claims it will distill agentic capabilities into smaller models, such as an upcoming 3B version. On base-model benchmarks, the card shows 66.9 on MMLU-Pro against 59.3 for Gemma4-31B-Base. Those figures belong to the base model and are separate from the reasoning model's Intelligence Index result.

According to recent reports, the two models reach 20 by different routes. Nanbeige scores 30% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 6% for Qwen, and 16% on the CritPt v2 Hard Subset against 4%. It also edges Qwen on AutomationBench-AA, 53% to 48%.

According to recent reports, elsewhere, it falls behind. On AA-Briefcase v1.1 it scores 1162 Elo against 1391, on FrontierCode 2.0 11% against 15%, and on HLE-Diamond 7% against 15%. The knowledge test tells the most distinctive story. On AA-Omniscience v1.1, Nanbeige scores -4 against Qwen's -6, with an 18% hallucination rate against 29%. Yet it answers only 29% of questions against 43%, declines 71% of them and gets 12% correct against 17%.

For general question answering, Qwen's higher accuracy is the better result.

According to recent reports, output tokens aren't a vanity metric. A reasoning model writes out its thinking as tokens, and every one costs decode time. If both models ran at the same speed on the same hardware, Nanbeige would take about 44% longer to finish a typical task.

According to recent reports, local decoding adds a second factor. Generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth, because each newly introduced token requires reading the model's weights, and a 33B dense model reads about 20% more weight data per token than a 27B dense model. Assuming the same quantization and the same memory-bound hardware, those two effects compound to roughly 1.7 times the wall-clock time per task. That figure is a back-of-the-envelope calculation, not a measured result.

It has been revealed that nor is there a hosted alternative to soften the blow. Artificial Analysis lists no confirmed public first-party or third-party APIs for Nanbeige, so unlike Qwen, which is sold per token through Alibaba's API, the cost is the hardware you run it on and the time it takes.

Industry observers note that artificial Analysis describes the model as small enough to run locally on a laptop, which holds true with a caveat. The weights are published in BF16, which at 33 billion parameters means roughly 66 GB, far beyond almost any laptop. At 8-bit, the weights fall to about 33 GB, and at 4-bit to about 17 GB, plus memory for the context cache. A machine with 24 GB of unified memory or more can plausibly hold a 4-bit build, though a long context will push it.

In a recent development, the vendor's own quickstart points the other way. The card's SGLang and vLLM examples both set tensor parallelism across four GPUs, which suggests the reference deployment is a multi-GPU server. Its Transformers example also enables trust_remote_code=True, which runs code from the repository. Reading that code first is the safer move, as is serving the model through vLLM or SGLang instead.

According to recent reports, quantization changes the model, too. The Intelligence Index numbers come from Artificial Analysis's own runs, so a 4-bit local build may score somewhat lower, or generate different token counts, than the version they evaluated.

According to recent reports, this release is a clean example of why a headline score isn't enough. Nanbeige delivers Qwen-level results at 33B, with strengths in terminal tasks and physics reasoning and a more cautious answering style. The price for those strengths is length.

Anyone choosing between the two should run both on their own workload and record three numbers: the score on their tasks, output tokens per task and seconds per task on their hardware. For terminal-heavy, agentic work, Nanbeige's profile may justify the longer runs. For knowledge-heavy or latency-sensitive work, Qwen's shorter, more accurate answers look stronger.

According to recent reports, three signals are worth watching next: whether the 3B distilled version keeps the model's strengths, whether other labs report the same token behavior, and whether anyone publishes quantized local benchmarks. Until then, the simplest summary is also the most accurate: same score, different bill.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Flop Labs has announced a minor delay to the launch of its public testnet, pushing back from its previous goal of 15:00 (UTC+8) on November 24.

It's unclear what the reason for the delay is, although the team does expect to launch the testnet before 18:00 (UTC+8) the same day.

Industry observers note that possible reasons for the delay could include conducting final checks, calibrating nodes, validator onboarding, load testing, etc. (although Flop Labs has not confirmed any of these to be the reason for the delay).

It does not appear that Flop Labs has any intends to move the testnet launch to another day.

Industry observers note that flop Labs is building FLOP Network, a blockchain serving as a settlement layer for what it calls the "agentic economy". This would enable AI agents to make payments for computation (e.g. model inference) and memory services, and provide rewards to GPU miners that contribute their computational power to fulfill these requests.

Computation is verified via Flop Labs' "Proof of Useful Inference", which entails miners providing evidence that they've carried out the desired AI computation, and validators checking this evidence.

Sources indicate that why does this matter? FLOP Network would enable agents to make payments for computation, memory, etc. Flop Labs' main competitors include Akash Network and io.net (both of which facilitate access to compute/gpu resources in a decentralized manner), as well as Render Network (which started out facilitating decentralized graphics rendering but has since expanded into AI/compute more broadly).

While Flop Labs' competitors also facilitate access to compute, Flop Labs' main differentiating factor appears to be its focus on facilitating agent-to-agent commerce and computation-verification.

Sources indicate that flop Labs is led by Arthur Hayes, co-founder of crypto exchange BitMEX and current chief investment officer at Maelstrom. The rest of Flop Labs' team includes Sergey Vidyuk (ex-Deutsche Bank/BitMEX) as CTO, and Shu Duan (with experience in investment banking and crypto asset management) as chief strategy officer.

The testnet would be an opportunity to see if Flop Labs can successfully build out its envisioned agentic economy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Album VC, a Lehi, Utah-based early-stage venture firm that’s been known until now as Peak Ventures, just gathered up $75 million in capital commitments for its third early-stage fund.

The development indicates investor confidence in Album’s young team, which came together in 2014 after the founder of Zinch — a site connecting colleges and students that sold to the ed-tech firm Chegg in 2011 — decided to try his hand at investing in other startups.

Industry observers note that as that founder, Sid Krommenhoek — who stayed on with Chegg for several years, running its international efforts — explains it, “I thought I’d do another startup. But I also knew from our own experience in struggling to raise money the need for more capital in Utah, and I thought having that operator-entrepreneur perspective could be useful.”.

A first fund, like many in the industry, was more of an experiment, though it was a decent $23 million, thanks largely to the support of Chegg CEO Dan Rosensweig, who was early to commit capital to the fund. A second ($56 million) fund followed when Krommenhoek and John Mayfield — a friend who joined him from a marketing role at Qualtrics — began investing more seriously in their backyard and beyond.

According to recent reports, they were soon joined by a third investor, Diogo Myrrha, who began as a principal with the firm and is now a general partner. Your AI Startup’s Exit Is Being Shaped By The Deals You Sign Today

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1094 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Valuations for AI companies have soared, and the companies are moving faster than ever.
  • Across the broader private market, Crunchbase’s Current Valuation Model estimates that the more than 1,900 startups on its Unicorn Board are worth about $2 trillion more collectively than their last reported funding-round valuations.
  • When everything moves that fast, the terms of your financings and of your contracts for compute, data and distribution get set early and in a hurry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Aaron Rubin and Greg Volkmar.

Valuations for AI companies have soared, and the companies are moving faster than ever. In the financings our firm has worked on so far in 2026, AI companies raised at median pre-money valuations up to 2.5 times those of non-AI companies from seed through Series C.

Across the broader private market, Crunchbase’s Current Valuation Model estimates that the more than 1,900 startups on its Unicorn Board are worth about $2 trillion more collectively than their last reported funding-round valuations.

When everything moves that fast, the terms of your financings and of your contracts for compute, data and distribution get set early and in a hurry. Some of those terms will later slow a sale, add cost and erode value. The key is making sure you take long enough to consider what a deal does to your exit before you sign.

Take license-and-hire deals, where a buyer licenses your technology and hires your team instead of acquiring the firm. They’ve become more common in AI, and the National Venture Capital Association has responded by updating its model charter. In 2025, it added an optional investor approval right over these deals, and sign-off by the board, including the investors’ directors, was enough to satisfy it.

Recent findings suggest that the November 2026 upgrade requires a vote of the preferred stockholders instead. Investors are often reluctant to use an approval right to block a deal. But it puts them at the negotiating table when an offer arrives, with a voice in how the proceeds are split between retention packages for the team and the cap table.

The stakes are higher when an investor is also a strategic partner. Nvidia and its NVentures investment arm alone have invested in more than 260 startups since the beginning of 2024, including 121 this year alone, Crunchbase data reveals.

Sources indicate that strategic capital often comes tied to compute, cloud or distribution agreements. Those agreements can carry exclusivity, change-of-control and right-of-first-negotiation terms, and a right of first negotiation can force you to put a competing bidder on ice while you talk to your strategic investor first.

Be realistic about your leverage. Terms from the hottest AI rounds get cited as “market,” but what you can get depends on how much investors want your deal. Spend your negotiating capital on the few provisions that will matter most in a sale instead of trying to optimize on marginal topics.

An AI company’s most valuable assets are often the hardest to diligence.

Recent findings suggest that start with data. A buyer will want to know where your training data came from and whether your contractual rights cover how you use it and how the buyer prepares to use it. Publicly available data isn’t necessarily licensed data. And permission to use a customer’s data to serve that customer doesn’t always cover training models for everyone else. If you fine-tuned on customer data under contracts that limit its use to serving those customers, a buyer may not be able to fold your models into its own products. The buyer may ask for a special indemnity, a larger escrow or a lower purchase price.

Your code gets similar scrutiny. In our deals, investors, and especially acquirers, now ask how much of the codebase was written with AI tools and whether those tools pulled in copyleft or commercially licensed code. We tell clients to audit their code regularly and fix concerns as they surface. It makes that diligence conversation far easier.

It has been revealed that compute and model-provider contracts raise a different problem: a buyer may inherit a commitment it doesn’t want. Minimum-spend commitments, reserved capacity and exclusivity terms generally stay with the company in a sale. A buyer with its own GPUs may have no use for three more years of your reserved capacity, and it will factor the remaining payments into its offer.

All of this is easier to fix at the negotiating table than in the middle of a buyer’s diligence.

• Map who decides on a sale. Know which board and investor approvals it would trigger, including any approval right over a license-and-hire deal.

• Track your data and code rights. Record data sources and use restrictions and audit AI-generated code periodically.

• Stress-test your infrastructure commitments. Run cloud, GPU and model-provider obligations against slower growth and a sale.

According to recent reports, • Keep strategic rights narrow. Limit the scope, duration and triggers of any right of first offer or negotiation you give a strategic investor.

It has been revealed that • Read commercial contracts with an exit in mind. Check the change-of-control and termination rights before you sign.

Few founders are thinking about a sale when they close a seed round or sign their first GPU contract. You don’t have to predict the exit. You do have to know what you’re giving up each time you sign, so the speed that got you funded doesn’t cost you flexibility when the right acquisition offer arrives.

He advises AI companies on strategic partnerships, technology and data licensing, and the development, commercialization, and deployment of AI products and services. His practice spans complex commercial transactions, intellectual property and data rights, and the evolving legal and regulatory problems shaping the AI industry. He also advises leading investors in industry-defining AI financings, including investments in Anthropic, OpenAI, and Databricks.

In a recent development, greg Volkmar is head of Gunderson Dettmer’s Newly introduced York corporate group and co-chairs the firm’s growth equity practice. For more than 20 years, Volkmar has focused on advising early- and late-stage technology and life science companies through financings, corporate governance, and securities law matters. He is also a trusted advisor to leading venture capital, private equity and crossover funds on their US and global investment activities, such as equity and debt financings, mergers and acquisitions, and secondary liquidity transactions, as well as fund formation needs.

Industry News: Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk.
  • “Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk.

“Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.

That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.

Recent findings suggest that but now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown claims, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.”.

It has been revealed that huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China.

After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of company secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap.

And typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said.

According to recent reports, honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.”.

Industry observers note that what’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others.

“Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch.

Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail.

Recent findings suggest that another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a proposal. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls.

“AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.”.

The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown stated.

“Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.”.

In a recent development, carpenter said a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information.

Industry observers note that bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown mentioned. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?”.

It also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he said, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the manufacturer.

Brown added that tech giant culture plays another role, too: Are employees comfortable with raising concerns, challenging unusual requests, and escalating possible threats? “One of the most dangerous security cultures is one where nobody feels comfortable questioning the CEO,” Carpenter mentioned.

“Founders need to take risks, and they need to explore business opportunities,” Brown stated. “Paranoia doesn’t help. Recognizing you’re a target does.”.

Crypto wallet provider Trezor has issued a security warning to cryptocurrency users following a recent theft report: "Never type your wallet backup into a phone, app or website.".

Recent findings suggest that according to Onchain Lens, a user reported losing over $600,000 across TRON and Solana while using an iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 27.2.1. Both the Trezor Safe 7 and the Exodus wallet were reportedly affected. The victim had been using a Trezor Safe 7 for nearly two months.

Industry observers note that according to the victim, the Trezor wallet arrived sealed, with no visible tampering; the recovery phrase was generated on the Trezor screen and not on the iPhone; the seed was written on paper and never stored digitally. The victim used Trezor Suite on an iPhone 17 Pro Max via Bluetooth and also had the Exodus wallet on the same iPhone.

The device was running iOS 27.2.1, and the victim never approved the unauthorized transactions. The Trezor wallets for TRON and Solana shared one recovery phrase.

Industry observers note that the user said $580,000 was stolen from Trezor on TRON and that an unauthorized transaction moved 49,999 USDT on Nov. 21, 2026. The transaction used the default owner permission, making the signing authority central to the investigation.

Another $23,400 was drained from Trezor on Solana, and the victim claims they never approved that transfer using the hardware device. The iPhone remains the main focus, as both Trezor Suite and Exodus were reportedly used on the same iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 27.2.1, and both were affected.

Industry observers note that trezor is designed to keep private keys inside the hardware device. However, compromising the phone alone should not normally provide access to Trezor's private keys, and the mechanism behind both thefts remains largely unknown.

According to recent reports, on November 9, 2026, Apple issued iOS 27.2.1, which patched several security holes (including some related to Bluetooth). The victim was reportedly running this version when the theft occurred. Thus, there is right now no evidence connecting those vulnerabilities to these transactions. Possible causes outlined included compromised recovery credentials, unauthorized signing, or a device or software security failure.

Trezor responded to this disclosure, saying that Trezor wallets don’t get drained out of nowhere and that there are presently no reports of funds being stolen remotely from any device. It noted that similar cases usually trace back to a compromised wallet backup.

It has been revealed that @OnchainLens @binance @Bybit_Official UPDATE: This device came directly from Trezor and highlights no sign of an implant. We’re still investigating what happened. So far there’s no confirmed loss of funds from implants and no implant found in any Trezor Safe 7. Never type your wallet backup into a phone, app or website.

It has been revealed that in a further update, Trezor confirmed that the device affected came directly from the tech giant and demonstrated no sign of an implant. The wallet provider added that it continues to investigate what happened.

This appears to be a standalone case, as Trezor reiterated that, so far, no confirmed loss of funds from implants has been reported, and no implant has been found in any Trezor Safe 7. It also reiterated an crucial security warning: users should never enter their wallet backups into a phone, application, or website.

#110445. Supertake raises $20M to let AI agents turn your market predictions into stock portfolios

Supertake raises $20M to let AI agents turn your market predictions into stock portfolios

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that AI investing startup Supertake has an interesting premise: What if your “takes” on the market could make you money without you having to pick stocks yourself?
  • It has been revealed that now, the tech giant has raised $20 million in seed funding to grow its business.
  • Industry observers note that michael Mignano originally incubated the startup at USV.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that AI investing startup Supertake has an interesting premise: What if your “takes” on the market could make you money without you having to pick stocks yourself? The service lets people turn their ideas into real investment portfolios, using frontier AI models and trading agents.

It has been revealed that now, the tech giant has raised $20 million in seed funding to grow its business. The round was led by venture firm Adjacent (Nico Wittenborn), with participation from Coinbase Ventures and Union Square Ventures (USV). Numerous angel investors also joined, including Nat Friedman, who’s currently head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs; Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch; renowned product manager Nikita Bier; investor Scott Belsky; and Nemil Dalal, a former Coinbase exec who is now a visiting partner at Y Combinator.

Industry observers note that michael Mignano originally incubated the startup at USV. He is the co-founder and former CEO of the podcasting platform Anchor, which Spotify acquired in 2019 for over $150 million. After leading Spotify’s podcasting business as “Head of Talk” for a few years, he joined the team at Lightspeed as a venture partner, betting on AI companies like Suno and Granola. He also co-founded Oboe, an AI education startup, and joined USV as a general partner in April.

According to recent reports, “We really believed there was an opportunity to make investing more democratized…and give everyone and anyone the ability to invest in their own insights and beliefs and ideas,” Mignano mentioned. While he will continue in his role as founder and executive chairman, he’s now brought in a team to run the company day to day.

Industry observers note that the team includes co-founders Lincoln Murr (CEO) and John Peterson (CTO). Both joined from Coinbase, where, Mignano notes, they were the heads of AI product and engineering, leading launches like Coinbase advisor, Coinbase for agents, agentic wallets, and others.

Industry observers note that the startup arrives as AI continues to make inroads into financial services, but allowing AI to take over people’s actual investments requires a new level of trust. Supertake is betting that people will ultimately be willing to take that leap, given recent improvements in frontier AI models.

Currently, Supertake works with Coinbase and Robinhood, and the company intends to expand to more brokerages over time. The idea is that you can explain, in broad, natural language, what you believe about how the world is going to change, and Supertake’s AI will iterate with you back and forth to turn that idea into a “take” that’s investable.

Under the hood, the startup is leveraging frontier AI technology and tools, combined with its own proprietary software that directs and limits what the AI can do.

Supertake’s users’ ideas are tracked on a leaderboard on the site, so others who agree can invest alongside them. For instance, there’s at the moment an idea on the leaderboard about looksmaxxing and longevity becoming more of a trend, where the portfolio includes certain pharma and cosmetic companies that could potentially benefit.

For now, these portfolios consist of stock picks, but the team wants to expand the service over time to handle other types of transactions, like shorts, derivatives, perpetuals, long exposure, or even prediction markets — the latter handled through partnerships with companies in that space.

Despite these “takes” seeming like bets on what could happen next in a given market, Murr stresses that this doesn’t make Supertake itself a prediction market.

Industry observers note that “We think it’s a novel and very much improved way to create what was previously considered the robo-advisor experience,” he notes. “When that came out, it had this amazing vision and direction of allowing people to have digital asset management. We think now is actually the time for that, with AI agents being so widely proliferated.”.

“I don’t think this is necessarily a prediction market by any means. The idea of natural language translation into an underlying set of assets feels different in that regard,” he says.

Still, the startup could wade into short-term predictions if a user’s take involves something they believe could happen in the near future, like who might win an election.

“We’re primarily focused on the longer, medium-term holdings today. But that being stated, we don’t want to preclude people from building out very hyper short-term strategies that might exist,” Murr adds.

To address people’s concerns over AI managing their money, Supertake’s team notes it’s implementing certain guardrails and spend limits. For instance, the AI has no ability to deposit or withdraw funds on a user’s behalf without their explicit consent. There are also drift limits in place so the portfolio stays balanced, plus allow and deny lists (meaning which assets the AI may and may not trade), real-time monitoring for anomalous activity, tools to set trade size limits, and a restriction that keeps agents from seeing the user’s brokerage credentials.

Recent findings suggest that “We view it as somewhat analogous to self-driving cars, actually, where there is a spectrum here of both trust and technological innovations that are happening,” says Murr. “Where a few years ago you may not feel comfortable getting in a car that has lane assist, but today you get in a Waymo, and it’s like nothing. And we think that there’s a very similar progression happening with the agentic finance space, and we’re far further along in the technological spectrum than people think.”.

Sources indicate that access to Supertake is still behind a waitlist while in beta, but the founders remarked they’ve put their money where their mouths are. Murr and Peterson are letting it manage “tens of thousands” and “thousands” of dollars, respectively.

Mignano, meanwhile, says he has Supertake managing “hundreds of thousands” of dollars.

With the latest funding, which follows a $2 million pre-seed round, Supertake aims to expand its team in areas like engineering, design, growth marketing, and others. Mignano and Murr are in New York, while Peterson is in the Austin area but commutes to New York at times. The team notes it hopes to figure out a hybrid work model as it grows.

Five Forged Receipts Drained $304.5K From Ankr's Ethereum Bridge Using a 0.0044 ankrETH Deposit

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1055 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, slowMist says five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit.
  • Recent findings suggest that on November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge.
  • All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, slowMist says five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit. Here is how the check failed.Every one of the five receipts was signed by the bridge's own trusted signer. Every one pointed to a deposit that had already been paid out.

Recent findings suggest that on November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge. According to SlowMist's alert, the attacker built five forged receipts that all referenced a single legitimate Optimism transaction, changing the recipient, the token and the withdrawal amount in each one.

All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.

Industry observers note that the reused transaction was tiny: a deposit of about 0.0044 ankrETH made on Optimism on November 3, which SlowMist's analysis says had already been redeemed on Ethereum the same day. Six days later, that one settled deposit was cited five times. The incident is recorded in the SlowMist Hacked database.Blockaid flagged the exploit as it unfolded, at about 08:42 UTC, with roughly $292,000 already gone. SlowMist followed at 09:14 UTC with the higher $304,500 estimate and an explanation of the forged receipts. Ankr paused withdrawals, and no recovery initiative has been confirmed.

The design is common across lock-and-release bridges. A user deposits on the source chain, and an off-chain set of signers watches for that deposit and signs a receipt describing it. The destination contract, in this case Ankr's Ethereum bridge contract, checks that the receipt carries a valid signature and then releases the funds.That setup makes the signers the source of truth. The contract can't see Optimism, so it leans on the signature to prove the deposit happened. The weak point sits in the gap between "the signer signed this" and "this really happened." A contract that treats the first as proof of the second inherits every mistake the signing process makes.

In a recent development, the Ethereum transactions show the attacker extracted about 82.91 ankrETH, 515,206 ankrPOL and 7.98 million ANKR tokens. Blockaid described the five withdraw calls as using the tiny Optimism deposit to unlock the bridge's locked inventory and send it to a newly introduced wallet.The mix of assets tells its own story. Each forged receipt named a different token and amount, which suggests the attacker picked targets based on what the bridge held. That fits receipts built entirely by the attacker, apart from the one real transaction reference. Anyone wanting to trace them can open the bridge contract's transaction list on Etherscan and filter for the five `withdraw` calls on November 9.

The most vital fact is still missing. SlowMist says the origin of the unauthorized signatures is under investigation, and it hasn't confirmed whether the signers were compromised.A valid signature on a forged receipt has a short list of explanations. A signing key, or the service holding it, could have been accessed. A signing service could have been tricked into signing attacker-supplied data. Or the signing logic itself could have a flaw that produces signatures for receipts it shouldn't. Each one points to a different fix: a stolen key means rotating signers, a manipulated service means tightening input validation off-chain, and a logic flaw means rewriting the signing rules.Whichever it turns out to be, the on-chain contract and the off-chain signer both failed to ask the same question. Either one verifying the source event would likely have stopped the attack, and neither did.

It has been revealed that the lessons are narrow and practical. Replay protection should key on the immutable identity of the source event, not on the receipt's contents, and a source event should be consumable exactly once. The destination contract should confirm that the receipt's recipient, token and amount match what the source-chain event actually recorded, using a proof or an independent verifier instead of trusting the signer alone.Signer infrastructure needs its own scrutiny. Threshold schemes, hardware-backed keys and strict limits on what a signing service will sign all shrink the damage from a single failure. Rate limits and per-withdrawal caps help as well. A bridge that can release its entire locked inventory in five calls has no brake once a signature check is defeated.Trust in a bridge comes in layers, and one layer rarely holds up alone. Users with funds in Ankr's bridge should watch for the project's post-mortem and its strategy for restoring withdrawals. For developers, the question to put to their own code is a blunt one: if a signer signs something false, what stops the contract from believing it?

Solana Validators Can Now Stop Block Processing

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, this PR proposes changes to validator software to help prevent work from being done.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In periods of competing blocks, Solana validators spend CPU and timing resources replaying blocks that will never make it into the canonical chain once another competing block from the same slot has been finalized.

According to recent reports, this PR proposes changes to validator software to help prevent work from being done. It also decouples functionality and gives control to Votor in requesting slot cancellation without modifying BankForks.

Sources indicate that overall, this is a reasonable technical improvement and has a good engineering motivation. Further technical comments and review would be helpful to understand if there are potential race conditions or challenges with reliability of replay and consensus. This could be split into two PRs to make it easier to test and review.

There are two main proposed changes:.

Make sure that the replay thread doesn't block on the scheduler finishing processing blocks.

Add slot cancellation, where Votor can tell replay which blocks to stop trying to process.

There was an earlier PR (PR #16454) which attempted to solve a similar problem, but that PR included some complexity around being able to pause and resume block processing.

This PR attempts to solve a similar problem in a simpler way by adding slot cancellation. It allows validators to stop replaying blocks that will never make it into the canonical chain once another block from the same slot has been finalized.

This is an efficiency-focused change to validator software. It's not intended to have a particular effect on transaction throughput or SOL price. For Solana to continue to perform well, it's important not only to continue to increase TPS but also continue to find ways to make sure that validators aren't doing unnecessary work.

For everyday users, it's unlikely there would be noticeable effects from this change. Sending/receiving SOL, using a DEX, using DeFi more broadly, and using any other Solana-powered website/app should all continue to function as normal. It's possible that users could see some benefits from this change in the form of Solana being more performant in the face of heavy compute loads.

The Art of The Terrible Startup Name

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When thinking of startup names, the usual question is how one identifies a great one.
  • But perhaps equally crucial is the reverse consideration: What makes for a truly awful startup name?
  • Industry observers note that it’s a somewhat subjective exercise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When thinking of startup names, the usual question is how one identifies a great one.

But perhaps equally crucial is the reverse consideration: What makes for a truly awful startup name?

Industry observers note that it’s a somewhat subjective exercise. Nonetheless, branding experts and occasional writers on the subject can agree on a few basic parameters. These include hard-sounding names, brands with negative connotations, and a certain ubiquitous suffix that could soon sound irrelevant.

Below, we look at each of these categories in more detail.

Sources indicate that one branding principle is that startups should avoid names that are unpleasant to pronounce. This includes words that sound too harsh or guttural, or are awkward in the native languages of potential users.

Unfortunately, it’s a principle often ignored.

Recent findings suggest that for Athol Foden of naming consultancy Brighter Naming, the most prominent unpleasant brand name of recent quarters is Grok, the chatbot of Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Foden hates it so much he devoted an entire essay to what’s wrong with it.

“I still want to throw up when you say that name… and it is even worse in foreign languages,” he said in an interview. In his essay he called the brand a cross between “a suppressed swear word and a throat condition your doctor would prescribe antibiotics for.”.

It’s not an anti-Musk stance. Foden is a fan of the entrepreneur’s Starlink as a name choice for the global satellite Internet service. It’s memorable and evocative in a positive way.

Recent findings suggest that for other examples, we didn’t want to pick on current startups for their naming choices. So we looked instead to archives of startups past for other cases of harsh naming choices that didn’t pan out or are no longer operating under that brand.

According to recent reports, our shortlist included Quibi, a heavily funded short video startup with famous founders and a famously short shelf life. Others that have either folded or no longer operate under the original brand include Doostang, Gtrot, and Xobni (inbox spelled backwards, but not terribly clear how to pronounce.).

Another naming tactic to avoid is selecting a brand that evokes negative imagery or connotations.

Industry observers note that “We always say: This is something you should be proud to wear on a hoodie,” said Bruno Benedini, co-founder of branding consultancy Taillight. If not, then reconsider.

Following this notion, one recently funded organization name that rubbed both Benedini and your author the wrong way is Warhound, a startup focused on breeding dogs for roles in the military, law enforcement and emergency response that recently raised $200 million.

Industry observers note that sure, it’s memorable. But it sets an awfully aggressive tone, especially for a pet-pampering culture in which other startups promote offerings like dog spas, canine couture, and custom meals. While there’s a role for well-treated service dogs, it’s preferably far from any battlefield.

Or, as Benedini put it, “I’d be embarrassed to have Warhound on my hoodie.”.

For other examples of less-than-stellar naming picks, we looked through the archives of startups past. One dud was Flud, which combines awkward spelling and imagery of a natural disaster. Boo.com, a defunct fashion site that was the iconic flops of the dot-com era also comes to mind, evoking fright more than the desire to shop. Another popular but questionable pick is Fire (sometimes alternately spelled Fyre), the chosen name of at least a dozen entries in the Crunchbase dataset.

According to recent reports, it may still be in vogue to give your tech giant a one-word name followed by AI. But don’t try to get a branding consultant to sign off on it.

It has been revealed that both Foden and Benedini advise against adding AI to the organization name for multiple reasons. One is that it will likely sound dated going forward. Another criticism is that since virtually every startup incorporates AI to some extent, adopting a name with “AI” isn’t particularly meaningful.

Industry observers note that if one does insist on an AI name, the minimum next step is to make sure it still works with those two letters on the end. Lots of companies — including Amazon (formerly Amazon.com) and Apple (initially Apple Computer) — have altered their names to keep up with the times and done just fine.

Sources indicate that despite all the advice on how to avoid an awful name, a part of me can’t help hoping more startups will just ignore it all. Then we could live in a world where startups sought funding with names like “Gruesome Grok AI” or “Festering Boil Labs.”.

That said, there’s a reason startup naming is a serious endeavor, and bad choices often have equally bad consequences.

Although XRP has begun to cool from the sudden price recovery witnessed at the beginning of the week that allowed it to reclaim the $1 price level, payment activity across its network has remained high.

After multiple days of extreme caution from traders, the latest on-chain data from XRPScan shows a sharp resurgence in payment volume on the XRP Ledger.

The data demonstrates that the total volume of XRP transferred between accounts on the XRP Ledger surpassed a massive 997.2 million XRP on November 23rd.

Further data shows that this marks an increase of about 370.1% in XRP payment volume over the last 24 hours; this means that the amount of XRP transferred between accounts has soared significantly after the major drop in activity seen the previous day.

The rapid spike in volume has drawn attention as it far exceeds the network's 30-day average payment volume of 791.8 million XRP.

While the surge has coincided with a sharp rebound in the price of XRP, it appears that transaction activity has picked up considerably as the market regains confidence.

It is crucial to note that the surge in XRP payment volume has come after XRP witnessed a parabolic price move, showing a daily increase of over 10% after reclaiming its $1 price level.

However, it appears that the rally has cooled as XRP has briefly fallen back into the red, retesting $0.9 once again.

Although its price movement has become weak again, on-chain data demonstrates that its network activity remains strong as holders continue to move the token across accounts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that cardano is under fire as Hoskinson defended the network’s utility amid a notable price fall. This came after New Zealand-based crypto trader and influencer Lark Davis revealed that Cardano’s real-world adoption remains despite being in existence for almost nine years.

According to recent reports, via his X account on Sunday, Nov. 22, Davis asked Cardano CEO Charles Hoskinson about looks to grow adoption on the network. With his huge crypto audience, the trader stated many users often ask him what has been holding Cardano back. As a result, he inquired why the protocol has failed to attract customers and capture meaningful market share. Compared with newer crypto networks like Solana, the analyst pointed out that Cardano’s daily active users and DeFi activity appear significantly low.

The Cardano founder suddenly emerged online on Sunday and responded to the celebrated trader. Hoskinson highlighted possible reasons, though with cautionary remarks. His answer hinted that a crypto network’s adoption is not determined by price, but by usage and transactions – indicators of real adoption.

In a recent development, according to Hoskinson, Cardano powers immense real-world on-chain use cases, financial applications, and tokenization utilities whose values are not directly measured by ADA price. He remarked Cardano’s infrastructure and applications are stronger than before, regardless of the ADA price.

He maintained that price doesn’t always show a network’s full capabilities. He added that different networks are on their own journeys and priorities, so comparing Solana with Cardano’s situation doesn’t make sense.

Recent findings suggest that despite Cardano launching four years earlier, its daily active customers are roughly 1% of Solana’s. Today, ADA trades at $0.1547, 95.3% down from its $3.09 peak reached five years ago in 2021.

Recent findings suggest that the question above about ADA and SOL highlights the battle for leadership in the crypto space. The two assets have emerged as two of the most popular chains, each with their own strengths and limitations.

According to recent reports, in terms of market value, Solana has vastly outpaced Cardano. As of today, SOL holds a market capitalization of $45.2 billion compared to ADA’s $5.7 billion. Besides that, Solana’s TVL at the moment reaches $$4.61 billion, significantly higher than Solana’s $43.14 million.

Industry News: Figma employee sues, alleging company forced her to confront harassers

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1372 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Figma engineer is suing the design software manufacturer and its co-founder and CEO, Dylan Field, over allegations that she faced sexual harassment and retaliation while managers and HR repeatedly told her to confront the very people she accused of misconduct.
  • District Court for the Southern District of Newly introduced York, alleges that Figma’s culture of “direct feedback” led managers and HR to make engineer Serry Park address harassment herself rather than investigate her complaints.
  • “Figma was my dream firm for a long time,” Park told TechCrunch in an interview before the lawsuit was filed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Figma engineer is suing the design software manufacturer and its co-founder and CEO, Dylan Field, over allegations that she faced sexual harassment and retaliation while managers and HR repeatedly told her to confront the very people she accused of misconduct.

The lawsuit, filed Monday in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Newly introduced York, alleges that Figma’s culture of “direct feedback” led managers and HR to make engineer Serry Park address harassment herself rather than investigate her complaints. Park, who joined Figma in 2022, alleges the firm’s response damaged her career, compensation, and mental health. The lawsuit also alleges that Park, who is Asian, faced racial and gender discrimination, including performance criticism based on stereotypes that Asian women are meek, timid, and conflict-averse.

“Figma was my dream firm for a long time,” Park told TechCrunch in an interview before the lawsuit was filed. “It was a place where I felt that I could level up in my career, working on a lot of really cool, interesting things at scale.”.

Park is seeking damages, a jury trial, and a court order prohibiting Figma from requiring employees who report harassment to confront their alleged harassers. She also wants the tech giant to adopt and enforce a process for investigating harassment complaints promptly and confidentially.

When reached for comment, a spokesperson for Figma mentioned, “Figma does not tolerate discrimination or harassment. Figma also does not tolerate extortion. These claims have no merit, and we will present the facts in court.”.

Park told TechCrunch she initially had faith in Figma’s complaint process, expecting that if she documented the alleged harassment and reported it to the right people, the company would act. But as an engineer in a male-dominated field, Park told TechCrunch, “I don’t feel that they took me seriously throughout this process.”.

Park, who is still employed at Figma, joined its San Francisco office in October 2022. Within weeks, her onboarding mentor — a fellow engineer — asked her on a date and continued pursuing her after she declined, Park alleges. She initially feared reporting him, worrying that her manager would “dismiss her reports or view her as the problem,” according to the lawsuit.

Park notes she tried to avoid her onboarding mentor. In early 2023, for example, she delayed choosing a work project until he had picked one. When her manager criticized her for not being a “team player,” Park explained that she was trying to avoid the colleague she accused of harassment, according to the suit.

Her manager allegedly dismissed her concerns, saying he had “met his wife at work too” and treating the behavior as “harmless flirtation.” When Park asked to be kept off projects with the onboarding mentor, HR allegedly instructed her to confront him directly about his behavior.

Sources indicate that the lawsuit ties that response to Figma’s culture of direct feedback, which Park alleges Field established and enforced. It indicates the manufacturer’s People organization trains managers to direct employees, including those reporting harassment, to give feedback directly to the person involved.

In a recent development, in March 2023, her manager assigned him to a major project she was leading, despite her request to be separated from him. Park told her manager that she would “figure it out,” but alleges that having to work with him affected her performance. Her manager gave her a 2 out of 5 on her performance review, criticizing her for not speaking up enough or engaging with others and for lacking presence. Park was put on a coaching plan, which she completed in late 2023.

According to recent reports, changing managers didn’t help, according to the lawsuit. Her second manager also refused to separate them, allegedly telling Park that someone at her level should be able to resolve conflicts with teammates and that separating them would be “avoiding the problem.” Like her previous manager, he allegedly pointed out that he had met his partner at work.

Park alleges the harassment continued throughout 2023.

In April 2024, she transferred to another team, a move she claims set back her career by resetting her performance and promotion timeline.

Sources indicate that on her fresh team, which had more women, Park noted she felt better and no longer had to work with her alleged harasser. Her performance reviews improved, but in late 2025, she alleges another incident of sexual harassment, this time by her new manager.

Recent findings suggest that the incident followed a night out for drinks with her wife and two teammates, including her manager. The next day, during a team lunch, the manager allegedly stated Park’s sex life had been discussed the previous evening. Park, who said no such conversation had occurred in her or her wife’s presence, felt “horrified and humiliated” by comments she believed fetishized queer relationships.

Sources indicate that A colleague reported the comments to HR as sexual harassment, according to the suit. Weeks later, Park’s manager apologized in a Slack message, saying she didn’t recall what she had said. When Park sought HR’s guidance, she was again told to address the matter directly with her manager.

During their conversation, the manager allegedly became defensive, and the encounter left Park feeling “crushed, anxious, and vulnerable.” The manager also allegedly said she would never make such a comment because she had “a lot of gay friends.”.

The manager told HR that they had agreed it was a misunderstanding. HR closed its investigation without interviewing witnesses, according to the suit, even though Park disputed her manager’s account.

“Requiring an employee to confront her harasser as the price of complaining — and then closing her complaint — would dissuade a reasonable employee from complaining at all,” the suit remarked.

Sources indicate that park alleges her manager retaliated by publicly berating her, sometimes so aggressively that colleagues intervened or checked on her afterward, according to the lawsuit. The suit also alleges that other teammates left the team over concerns about the manager’s behavior.

Park again complained to HR about “escalating retaliation” and expressed concern the manager would “derail her career.” HR allegedly defended the manager’s conduct, saying the manager was “within her reasonable authority” and again instructed Park to address her concerns directly with the manager.

Recent findings suggest that in early 2026, Park received another low performance review and a reduced bonus. The lawsuit alleges that similarly situated men continued to receive promotions, raises, and bonuses. When Park reported the negative performance review to HR in March, she was allegedly told her sexual harassment complaint against her manager could not be “substantiated.”.

In a recent development, park took medical leave in March to receive treatment for PTSD symptoms and generalized anxiety. Cleared to return to work in June, she was prescribed workplace accommodations, including a graduated work schedule and mandatory remote workdays.

Park told TechCrunch that Figma approved the accommodations but had not implemented them at the time she returned to work. In July, Park and her lawyers notified Figma of their intent to pursue legal action.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s really scary for me,” she stated about taking legal action. “I don’t know what’s going to happen next with this, I don’t know what the outcome is going to be, but at least it feels like this is my chance to do the right thing.”.

This piece was updated to clarify when Park remarked Figma implemented the recommendations from her medical professionals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic’s stock fell below its IPO price of $83, trading as low as $76 a share by midday Tuesday, down nearly 12% from Monday’s close.

Falling below the IPO price is often seen as a negative signal because underwriters typically price offerings at a discount to their expected trading value.

The AI industry has been eagerly watching how Anthropic’s shares trade, with VCs and other observers saying its performance could serve as a barometer for how public market investors value the sector.

According to recent reports, the dramatic slump comes less than a week after Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq at $111.50 a share. If its shares continue to trade poorly in the coming weeks, the slide could put pressure on private startup valuations and weaken IPO prospects for other AI companies.

Anthropic isn’t the only AI stock selling off on Tuesday. Nvidia fell more than 7% by midday, giving back some of the more than 30%-plus gain it posted Monday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bank of America sees the S&P 500 reaching 7,800 by the end of 2027.

The forecast comes after the index suffered an 11.62% correction from its October record.

Several major Wall Street banks have set higher 2027 targets than Bank of America.

Bank of America equity strategist Savita Subramanian sees the S&P 500 climbing back toward 7,800 by the end of 2027. The call comes after the index fell more than 11% from its October record.

The forecast comes as investors weigh AI earnings against inflation, valuations, weaker buybacks and a tougher market ahead.

The S&P 500 reached a record closing high of 7,818.93 on October 6, when the index was up about 14% for the year. But the rally swiftly lost momentum.

In a recent development, by November 20, the index had dropped to 6,910.39, marking an 11.62% decline from its record. It has since recovered, but remains about 7.9% below the October high.

$SPY – BANK OF AMERICA SEES S&P 500 AT 7,800 BY END OF 2027Bank of America strategist Savita Subramanian forecasts the S&P 500 reaching 7,800 by year-end 2027, implying approximately 8.3% upside from Tuesday's close.The bank outlines three scenarios:🔸 Bull case: 8,500🔸….

That pullback is now a key part of BofA’s 2027 outlook.

Strategist Savita Subramanian expects the index to reach 7,800, which would put it close to its previous record and represent about 8.3% upside from today’s level near 7,201.

BofA also sees three possible ranges, i.e 8,500 in a bull case, 7,800 in its base case, and 6,600 if the market turns sharply lower.

But BofA is not expecting an easy climb.

Subramanian expects S&P 500 earnings to grow by about 12% in 2027. The problem is that stronger profits may not translate into the same level of stock gains seen during the earlier rally.

BofA expects valuation multiples to come under pressure as buybacks weaken and companies issue more shares. That could limit how much investors are willing to pay for each dollar of earnings.

AI spending is another major factor. Massive investment in AI has helped support earnings expectations across the market, but uncertainty around the size and timing of those returns could keep stocks volatile.

BofA favors communication services, financials, health care and consumer discretionary stocks, while remaining cautious on consumer staples.

The bank also sees the recent correction creating buying opportunities, although it expects 2027 to be a more difficult market.

BofA’s 7,800 target sits below several other major Wall Street forecasts.

JPMorgan, UBS and Wells Fargo each see the S&P 500 at 8,200 in 2027. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are targeting 8,700, while Deutsche Bank has the highest forecast at 9,000.

The Bloomberg-compiled consensus stands at 8,471.

Maple raises $5.3M to build AI products that protect your data, even from itself

💡 Key Takeaways
